# Unipotent Representations and the Categorical Trace of Frobenius

**Authors:** Wyatt Reeves

## Abstract

We give a new proof of the classification of unipotent representations for split finite groups of Lie type. To do this, we first construct an $(\infty,2)$ -categorification of Lusztig’s map from the Hecke algebra to the asymptotic algebra. Then we use the theory of weights to show that it induces an isomorphism after applying trace of Frobenius.

## 1. Introduction

### 1.1. Motiviation

#### 1.1.1.

A basic problem in representation theory is to understand the category of representations of a group. When $\Gamma$ is a finite group and the field of coefficients has characteristic zero, a classical theorem of H. Maschke says that $\Rep(\Gamma)$ is semisimple. As a result, to describe the structure of $\Rep(\Gamma)$ in this case, it suffices to give a parameterization of the irreducible representations of $\Gamma$ .

#### 1.1.2.

In a sense, the most basic case where one can try to enumerate the irreducible representations of $\Gamma$ is when the group is simple and the field of coefficients is algebraically closed. If $\Gamma$ is $\mathbf{Z}/p$ then the answer is very simple, and if $\Gamma$ is one of the sporadic simple groups the irreducible representations can be enumerated by hand. If $\Gamma$ is the alternating group $A_{n}$ , then because of the short exact sequence

$$ 1\to A_{n}\to S_{n}\to\mathbf{Z}/2\to 1, $$

and the vanishing of $H^{2}(\mathbf{Z}/2;{\mathbf{G}_{m}})$ , it is relatively straightforward to describe the irreducible representations of $A_{n}$ in terms of those of $S_{n}$ . The classical work of G. Frobenius, A. Young, I. Schur, and A. Specht then provides a parameterization of the irreducible representations of the symmetric group $S_{n}$ in terms of partitions of $n$ .

The remaining finite simple groups are all of Lie type, meaning that there is a short exact sequence

$$ 1\to\Gamma\to G^{F}\to A\to 1 $$

where $G$ is a simple algebraic group of adjoint type defined over $\overline{\mathbf{F}}_{p}$ , $F:G\to G$ is a Steinberg endomorphism of $G$ (meaning that some power of $F$ is a Frobenius endomorphism of $G$ ), and $A$ is a finite abelian group. Like in the case of the alternating group, the key input needed to understand the representations of $\Gamma$ is an understanding of the representations of $G^{F}$ . For simplicity, we will restrict our attention to the case that $F$ is actually a Frobenius automorphism of $G$ : in this case the group $G^{F}$ identifies with $G(\mathbf{F}_{q})$ .

#### 1.1.3.

In the work of P. Deligne and G. Lusztig [DL76], it was shown that the irreducible representations of $G(\mathbf{F}_{q})$ fall into families parameterized by semisimple elements in $\check{G}(\mathbf{F}_{q})$ up to geometric conjugacy, where $\check{G}$ denotes the Langlands dual group. The representations whose semsisimple parameter is $1\in\check{G}(\mathbf{F}_{q})$ are called unipotent. For a general semisimple element $s\in\check{G}(\mathbf{F}_{q})$ , a theorem of R. Steinberg and T. Springer [Ste63, Lemma 3.9.(2)] shows that the centralizer of $s$ is a connected reductive group. Furthermore, by the work of Lusztig [Lus84] (see also [LY20]) the category of representations of $G(\mathbf{F}_{q})$ with semisimple parameter $s$ is naturally equivalent to the category of unipotent representations of $H(\mathbf{F}_{q})$ , where $H$ is the Langlands dual group of $Z(s)$ (although $Z(s)$ may not be split even if $G$ is).

#### 1.1.4.

In [Lus84], Lusztig also showed that the irreducible unipotent representations of $G(\mathbf{F}_{q})$ themselves break into families parameterized by the two-sided cells of the Weyl group of $G$ . Furthermore, to each two-sided cell $c$ , one can attach a finite group $A_{c}$ such that the irreducible unipotent representations in the family associated to $c$ are parameterized by pairs $(x,\sigma)$ , where $x$ is an element of $A_{c}$ and $\sigma$ is an irreducible representation of the centralizer of $x$ in $A_{c}$ .

Despite the fact that Lusztig’s result can be stated uniformly in the group $G$ , the proof relies on extensive type-by-type calculations. This has the advantage of being very explicit, but it is natural to wonder whether there is a uniform proof of the classification of unipotent representations. The goal of this paper is to provide a uniform proof of a result which is slightly weaker than the one stated above. Namely, we will prove

#### Theorem 1.1.4 (Theorem 6.5.1).

The category $\Rep(G(\mathbf{F}_{q}))^{\mathrm{unip}}$ admits a direct sum decomposition indexed by two-sided cells

$$ \Rep(G(\mathbf{F}_{q}))^{\mathrm{unip}}\simeq\bigoplus_{c}\Rep(G(\mathbf{F}_{q}))^{\mathrm{unip}}_{c} $$

such that

$$ \Rep(G(\mathbf{F}_{q}))^{\mathrm{unip}}_{c}\simeq\QCoh_{\mathscr{G}}(A_{c}/A_{c}) $$

for a finite group $A_{c}$ and gerbe $\mathscr{G}$ .

As we have stated it, Lusztig’s classification follows from this theorem plus the knowledge that the gerbe $\mathscr{G}$ is always trivializable. Using the prior work of [LO14], it is easy to verify that in all cases the gerbe $\mathscr{G}$ is trivializable; unfortunately we cannot give a uniform proof of this fact. On the other hand, we should emphasize that even though $\mathscr{G}$ is always trivializable, it may not have a canonical trivialization. This causes the appearance of certain constant factors in the formulas for the characters of unipotent representations in types $E_{7}$ and $E_{8}$ (see [Ost14]).

We should caution that although we certainly expect that our partition of $\Rep(G(\mathbf{F}_{q}))^{\mathrm{unip}}$ into families agrees with that of [Lus84], we do not prove this. Additionally, our strategy for proving Theorem 1.1.4 is to first prove an equivalence

$$ \Rep(G(\mathbf{F}_{q}))^{\mathrm{unip}}_{c}\simeq HH(\mathscr{J}_{c}) $$

(using our definition of $\Rep(G(\mathbf{F}_{q}))^{\mathrm{unip}}_{c}$ ) and then apply the results of [LO14]. In [Lus15], Lusztig proves a statement equivalent to (1) (using his definition of $\Rep(G(\mathbf{F}_{q}))^{\mathrm{unip}}_{c}$ ), so in a sense the contribution of this paper is simply to give a new proof of this result. See §1.2.16 for more discussion.

### 1.2. Overview

#### 1.2.1.

The goal of this section is to give an overview of our proof of Theorem 1.1.4. Our point of departure is a recent result of A. Eteve [Ete25]. To state it, let’s introduce some notation: if $\mathscr{A}$ is a monoidal dg category and $\mathscr{M}$ is an $(\mathscr{A},\mathscr{A})$ -bimodule category, we will write $HH(\mathscr{A};\mathscr{M})$ for the category

$$ \mathscr{A}\underset{\mathscr{A}\otimes\mathscr{A}^{\mathrm{rev}}}{\otimes}\mathscr{M}. $$

As a special case, if $\phi$ is a monoidal automorphism of $\mathscr{A}$ , then we will write

$$ HH(\mathscr{A};\phi)=HH(\mathscr{A};\mathscr{A}_{\phi}) $$

where $\mathscr{A}_{\phi}$ is the $(\mathscr{A},\mathscr{A})$ -bimodule category where the right action of $\mathscr{A}$ has been twisted by $\phi$ .

If $G$ is a reductive group with Borel subgroup $B$ , let $\mathscr{H}$ denote the bi-equivariant Hecke category

$$ \mathscr{H}=\Sh(B\backslash G/B) $$

where $\Sh(-)$ denotes the dg category of ind-constructible $\overline{\mathbf{Q}}_{\ell}$ -sheaves. $\mathscr{H}$ is a monoidal category via convolution, and Eteve’s theorem shows that

$$ HH(\mathscr{H};\mathrm{Frob})\simeq\Rep(G(\mathbf{F}_{q}))^{\mathrm{unip}}. $$

(One caveat: this result doesn’t appear as stated in [Ete25], but it follows from [Ete25, Theorem 6.1.1] by setting the semisimple parameter to 1. Alternatively, one can deduce this equivalence from an even more recent and very general result of X. Zhu [Zhu25, Proposition 8.57], see §6.2.1 for more discussion.)

#### 1.2.2.

Let us now explain how the decomposition of unipotent representations into families indexed by two-sided cells arises from this point of view. Recall from [BZN15, Definition 1.4], [AGK+22, Appendix C] that a monoidal dg category $\mathscr{A}$ is said to be semi-rigid if

- (1) The multiplication map $\mathrm{mult}:\mathscr{A}\otimes\mathscr{A}\to\mathscr{A}$ admits a continuous $(\mathscr{A},\mathscr{A})$ -bilinear right adjoint.

- (2) $\mathscr{A}$ is dualizable.

In Construction 2.2.2, we show that in a high degree of generality, semiorthogonal decompositions of semi-rigid monoidal categories induce semiorthogonal decompositions after passing to $HH(-)$ . Because $\Rep(G(\mathbf{F}_{q}))^{\mathrm{unip}}$ is semi-simple, every semiorthogonal decomoposition of $\Rep(G(\mathbf{F}_{q}))^{\mathrm{unip}}$ is actually a direct sum decomposition.

In [BZN15, Theorem 1.8], D. Ben-Zvi and D. Nadler prove that the monoidal category $\mathscr{H}$ is semi-rigid, so to produce a direct sum decomposition of $\Rep(G(\mathbf{F}_{q}))^{\mathrm{unip}}$ indexed by two sided cells, it suffices to produce a system of semiorthogonal decompositions of $\mathscr{H}$ indexed by two-sided cells.

#### 1.2.3.

Let us now briefly recall the definition of two-sided cells. First, one defines a preorder on the Weyl group as follows: for any $w\in W$ , we can consider the full subcategory $\mathscr{H}_{w}^{\mathrm{access}}\subseteq\mathscr{H}$ which is the smallest cocomplete two-sided ideal containing $L_{w}$ ; say $v\leq_{LR}w$ if $L_{v}$ is contained in $\mathscr{H}_{w}$ . Using this preorder we may partition $W$ into subsets called two-sided cells by stipulating that $w$ and $v$ lie in the same two-sided cell when $v\leq_{LR}w$ and $w\leq_{LR}v$ . One can define left cells and right cells similarly, by replacing $\mathscr{H}_{w}$ with the smallest cocomplete left ideal (resp. right ideal) containing $L_{w}$ .

If $c$ is a two sided cell, then we will write $w\leq_{LR}c$ to mean $w\leq_{LR}v$ for some (equiv. any) $v\in c$ . We will also write $\mathscr{H}_{\leq c}^{\mathrm{access}}$ to refer to the category we called $\mathscr{H}_{w}^{\mathrm{access}}$ for $w\in c$ . There is also a different category that one can consider, which we simply denote $\mathscr{H}_{\leq c}$ . This is the subcategory of $\mathscr{H}$ consisting of objects such that all of the simple subquotients of all of their cohomology groups are of the form $L_{w}$ for $w\leq c$ . In general, $\mathscr{H}_{\leq c}$ is strictly larger than $\mathscr{H}_{\leq c}^{\mathrm{access}}$ , but every object of $\mathscr{H}_{\leq c}$ which is cohomologically bounded below lies in $\mathscr{H}_{\leq c}^{\mathrm{access}}$ (see §4.4.3 for more discussion of this point).

We should note that the two-sided order is traditionally defined purely combinatorially (see [KL79]). However, Soergel’s conjecture implies that the combinatorial definition agrees with the definition in terms of two-sided ideals in $\mathscr{H}$ (for finite Weyl groups, Soergel’s conjecture is a consequence of the decomposition theorem of [BBD82]; more generally see [EW14]).

#### 1.2.4.

The bounded-derived versions of the categories $\mathscr{H}_{\leq c}$ have been studied extensively (see [BFO12], [EW21]). However, an important feature of $\mathscr{H}_{\leq c}$ only appears at the level of unbounded derived categories: the inclusion $\mathscr{H}_{\leq c}\to\mathscr{H}$ admits a left adjoint (for this to be true it is necessary to consider $\mathscr{H}_{\leq c}$ rather than $\mathscr{H}_{\leq c}^{\mathrm{access}}$ ). This was first proved in the de Rham setting in [DF25] using the theory of degenerate Whittaker coefficients.11 1 Strictly speaking, the results of loc. cit. concern the categories $\mathscr{H}_{Z}$ obtained by imposing a singular support condition on the objects of $\mathscr{H}$ , but in the de Rham setting one can pass between two-sided cells and singular support conditions using [BV83, Theorem 1.1]. (See also [Tan88] for a nice overview.) In Proposition 4.1.3, we give a new proof of this result just using basic facts about category $\mathscr{O}$ . It follows that at the level of unbounded derived categories, we obtain a system of semiorthogonal decompositions

$$ \mathscr{H}_{\not\leq c}\rightleftarrows\mathscr{H}\rightleftarrows\mathscr{H}_{\leq c}, $$

and by Construction 2.2.2 this produces the desired direct sum decomposition of $\Rep(G(\mathbf{F}_{q}))^{\mathrm{unip}}$ into families.

These semiorthogonal decompositions of $\mathscr{H}$ are of fundamental importance for us, so let us briefly say what happens for $SL_{2}$ (see §4.1.2 for more discussion). The semiorthogonal decomposition of $\mathscr{H}$ arises from a similar semiorthogonal decomposition of (the unbounded derived category of) the principal block of category $\mathscr{O}$ . If we take $c$ to be the two-sided cell $\left\{s\right\}$ , where $s$ is the nontrivial element of the Weyl group, the subcategory $(\mathscr{O}_{0})_{\not\leq c}$ is just the full subcategory generated under colimits and shifts by the big projective, and $(\mathscr{O}_{0})_{\leq c}$ is the derived category of lisse sheaves on $\mathbf{P}^{1}$ . If $L_{1}$ is the delta sheaf on the closed Bruhat stratum, then this semiorthogonal decomoposition produces an exact triangle

$$ \tau_{\not\leq c}L_{1}\to L_{1}\to\tau_{\leq c}L_{1} $$

and one can show that

$$ H_{i}(\tau_{\leq c}L_{1})=\begin{cases}L_{s}&i\geq 1\\
0&i<1\end{cases} $$

and

$$ H_{i}(\tau_{\not\leq c}L_{1})=\begin{cases}L_{s}&i>0\\
\nabla_{s}&i=0\\
0&i<0\end{cases} $$

where $\nabla_{s}$ refers to the costandard object with socle $L_{s}$ .

#### 1.2.5.

Now that we have a decomposition

$$ \Rep(G(\mathbf{F}_{q}))^{\mathrm{unip}}\simeq\bigoplus_{c}\Rep(G(\mathbf{F}_{q}))^{\mathrm{unip}}_{c} $$

of the category of unipotent representations into families indexed by two-sided cells, we still need to describe the categories $\Rep(G(\mathbf{F}_{q}))^{\mathrm{unip}}_{c}$ . Note that if we pick a representative of each conjugacy class of $A_{c}$ , then we obtain an isomorphism of stacks

$$ A_{c}/A_{c}\simeq\bigsqcup_{[x]\in\Conj(A_{c})}*/Z_{A_{c}}(x), $$

so we can rephrase §1.1.4 as saying that there is an equivalence

$$ \Rep(G(\mathbf{F}_{q}))^{\mathrm{unip}}_{c}\simeq\QCoh(A_{c}/A_{c}). $$

On the other hand, by a uniform argument we will be able to show that

$$ \Rep(G(\mathbf{F}_{q}))^{\mathrm{unip}}_{c}\simeq\QCoh_{\mathscr{G}}(A_{c}/A_{c}) $$

for some gerbe $\mathscr{G}$ .22 2 As we have mentioned already, one can show by case-by-case calculations that $\mathscr{G}$ is non-canonically trivializable. We should caution that the group we are calling $A_{c}$ is defined quite inexplicitly (see §1.2.9, §1.3.2).

#### 1.2.6.

If $\Gamma$ is a finite group and $\omega\in H^{3}(\Gamma;{\mathbf{G}_{m}})$ is a cohomology class, then following [Qui98, §2.3.3] (see also [LO14, §3.1]) one can define a monoidal category

$$ \Vect_{\Gamma,\omega} $$

which agrees with $\QCoh(\Gamma)$ as a plain category, but whose associativity constraint is twisted by by $\omega$ . By [Fre94, §8], [Wil08],

$$ HH(\Vect_{\Gamma,\omega};\id)\simeq\QCoh_{\mathscr{G}}(\Gamma/\Gamma) $$

for a certain gerbe $\mathscr{G}$ constructed from $\omega$ . In fact, the gerbe on the right hand side of (2) arises in this way (for a certain cohomology class $\omega$ which we will return to in §1.2.9). It follows that we may rewrite (2) as an equivalence

$$ HH(\mathscr{H}_{c};\mathrm{Frob})\simeq HH(\Vect_{A_{c},\omega};\id). $$

#### 1.2.7.

To prove an equivalence like (3), it is useful to know that $HH(-)$ is a Morita invariant: if there is an equivalence of categories

$$ \mathscr{A}\textrm{-mod}\simeq\mathscr{B}\textrm{-mod}, $$

then $HH(\mathscr{A})\simeq HH(\mathscr{B})$ . More generally, if $\mathscr{A}$ and $\mathscr{B}$ are equipped with endomorphisms $\phi$ and $\psi$ , and the equivalence (4) intertwines the induced endofunctors of module categories,

$$ {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{A}\textrm{-mod}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{B}\textrm{-mod}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{A}\textrm{-mod}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{B}\textrm{-mod}} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{ind}_{\phi}} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\sim} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{ind}_{\psi}} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\sim} $$

then $HH(\mathscr{A};\phi)\simeq HH(\mathscr{B};\psi)$ .

These properties of $HH$ are easy to see from the point of view of categorical traces (see [BZN13, KP22, GKRV22]). Namely, for any symmetric monoidal category $\mathscr{C}$ and any dualizable object $x\in\mathscr{C}$ , there is a map

$$ \tr:\End(x)\to\End(1_{\mathscr{C}}) $$

which sends an endomorphism $\phi$ to $\tr(\phi;x)$ , defined to be the composite

$$ 1_{\mathscr{C}}\xrightarrow{\epsilon}x\otimes x^{\vee}\xrightarrow{\phi\otimes\id}x\otimes x^{\vee}\xrightarrow{\eta}1_{\mathscr{C}}. $$

For our purposes, one should take $\mathscr{C}=2\mathrm{dgCat}$ (see [GRV26]) and $x=\mathscr{A}\textrm{-mod}$ . Every $(\mathscr{A},\mathscr{A})$ -bimodule $\mathscr{M}$ defines an endomorphism of $\mathscr{A}\textrm{-mod}$ , and [GKRV22, §3.7.1] shows that

$$ HH(\mathscr{A};\mathscr{M})\simeq\tr(\mathscr{M};\mathscr{A}\textrm{-mod}). $$

#### 1.2.8.

Our proof of (3) passes through an intermediate object, Lusztig’s asymptotic category $\mathscr{J}_{c}$ (see [Lus97], [EW21, §5]). This is a semisimple monoidal category, whose simple objects $J_{w}$ are labelled by elements $w\in c$ . To describe the monoidal structure, we first have to recall the definition of Lusztig’s $a$ -function. By definition, for a two-sided cell $c$ , the number $a(c)$ is the smallest integer such that

$$ H^{i}(L_{w}*L_{v})\in\mathscr{H}_{<c} $$

for all $i>a(c)$ and $w,v\in c$ . The monoidal structure on $\mathscr{J}_{c}$ is defined so that

$$ J_{w}*J_{v}\simeq\bigoplus_{u\in c}J_{u}^{\oplus n_{u}} $$

where $n_{u}$ is the multiplicity of $L_{u}$ in $H^{a(c)}(L_{w}*L_{v})$ . Roughly speaking, $\mathscr{J}_{c}$ remembers the “leading term” of the monoidal structure of $\mathscr{H}_{c}$ .

#### 1.2.9.

We should now explain how $\mathscr{J}_{c}$ is related to both $\mathscr{H}_{c}$ and the category $\Vect_{A_{c},\omega}$ (which we have not yet fully defined!). Let’s begin with the relationship between $\mathscr{J}_{c}$ and $\Vect_{A_{c},\omega}$ , which is supplied by a theorem of I. Losev and V. Ostrik [LO14, Theorem 5.1]. Using the theory of finite $\mathscr{W}$ -algebras, Losev and Ostrik construct a module category $\mathscr{M}_{c}$ for $\mathscr{J}_{c}$ , with the property that

$$ \End_{\mathscr{J}_{c}}(\mathscr{M}_{c}) $$

is a group category, in the sense of [Qui98] (this means that the category is semisimple and every simple object is tensor invertible). This implies (by §2.3.2 of loc. cit.) that

$$ \End_{\mathscr{J}_{c}}(\mathscr{M}_{c})\simeq\Vect_{A_{c},\omega} $$

for some group $A_{c}$ and some $\omega\in H^{3}(A_{c};{\mathbf{G}_{m}})$ . We will take this as our definition of $A_{c}$ . Note that the group we call $A_{c}$ is denoted $\overline{\mathbf{A}}$ in [LO14]; they reserve the notation $A_{c}$ for a group which is defined in terms of Springer theory (see §1.3.2 for more discussion). In fact, Losev and Ostrik prove that $\mathscr{M}_{c}$ defines a Morita equivalence

$$ \mathscr{J}_{c}\textrm{-mod}\simeq\Vect_{A_{c},\omega}\textrm{-mod}. $$

Because $HH(-)$ is a Morita invariant, this implies that we may reformulate (3) as the following equivalence, which is the main result of this paper

#### Theorem 1.2.9 (Theorem 6.4.4).

$$ HH(\mathscr{H}_{c};\mathrm{Frob})\simeq HH(\mathscr{J}_{c};\id). $$

#### 1.2.10.

It is in some sense obvious from the definition that the asymptotic category $\mathscr{J}_{c}$ is related to the Hecke category $\mathscr{H}_{c}$ . However, one of the contributions of this paper is to articulate a new relationship between the two, which in fact supplies a new construction of $\mathscr{J}_{c}$ as a monoidal category. Namely, in [GLR26], D. Gaitsgory, K. Lin, and the author showed that the theory of weights gives rise to an action of the monoid $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ on a category $\Sh(X)^{\mathrm{relev}}$ for any scheme $X$ over $\mathbf{F}_{q}$ . Here the monoid structure on $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ is given by multiplication and the category $\Sh(X)^{\mathrm{relev}}$ is a certain full subcategory of the category $\Sh(X)$ of ind-constructible $\overline{\mathbf{Q}}_{\ell}$ -sheaves on $X$ .

It is not hard to extend this construction to Artin stacks, and when $X=B\backslash G/B$ every ind-constructible sheaf lies in $\Sh(X)^{\mathrm{relev}}$ . We therefore obtain an action of $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ on $\mathscr{H}$ , and in §4.3 we show that this induces an action of $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ on $\mathscr{H}_{c}$ such that $\mathscr{J}_{c}$ is simply the category of invariants,

$$ \mathscr{J}_{c}\simeq\mathscr{H}_{c}^{\mathbf{A}^{1}}. $$

We think of this as a precise articulation of the slogan that says that $\mathscr{J}_{c}$ is the limit of $\mathscr{H}_{c}$ as $v$ goes to zero.

#### 1.2.11.

With the results of the previous paragraphs in mind, it remains to prove an equivalence

$$ HH(\mathscr{H}_{c};\mathrm{Frob})\simeq HH(\mathscr{H}_{c}^{\mathbf{A}^{1}};\id). $$

This occupies the bulk of our paper. Let’s describe a toy model for our argument: if $A$ is a non-negatively graded algebra and $\mathrm{act}_{\lambda}$ is the automorphism of $A$ that rescales the $i$ th weight space by $\lambda^{i}$ , then whenever $\lambda$ isn’t a root of unity,

$$ HH(A;\mathrm{act}_{\lambda})\simeq HH(A_{0};\id), $$

where $A_{0}$ is the zeroth graded piece of $A$ . The argument is simple: note that $A$ is acted on by the monoid $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ , and $A_{0}=A^{\mathbf{A}^{1}}$ is the ring of fixed points for this action. Then because $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ is commutative, the $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ -action on $A$ induces an action on $HH(A;\mathrm{act}_{\lambda})$ , and the fixed points of this action are

$$ HH(A_{0};\mathrm{act}_{\lambda})=HH(A_{0};\id). $$

Now note the action of $\lambda$ on $HH(A;\mathrm{act}_{\lambda})$ is canonically trivial. As a consequence, whenever $\lambda$ is not a root of unity (and therefore the powers of $\lambda$ are Zariski dense in $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ ), the action of $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ on $HH(A;\mathrm{act}_{\lambda})$ is trivial, so $HH(A;\mathrm{act}_{\lambda})$ is equal to its $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ -fixed points.

To relate our desired equivalence (5) to this toy model, we need to explain why the Frobenius automorphism of $\mathscr{H}_{c}$ has the form $\mathrm{act}_{\lambda}$ for some $\lambda$ . In §6.1 we show that this follows from W. Soergel and M. Wendt’s motivic construction of the Hecke category [SW18]. As a result, roughly speaking, our equivalence (5) is just a categorified version of the equivariant localization isomorphism (6). However, several problems arise when we try to make this precise.

#### 1.2.12.

The most serious problem with viewing the equivalence (5) as an instance of equivariant localization is the fact that the $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ -action on $\mathscr{H}_{c}$ of §1.2.10 is only laxly compatible with the monoidal structure on $\mathscr{H}_{c}$ . As a result, it is unclear why there should be an actual $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ -action on $HH(\mathscr{H}_{c};\mathrm{Frob})$ . However, we are able to get around this problem by introducing a new monoidal category

$$ \mathscr{B}_{c}=\gr_{0}(1_{c})\mathrm{-bimod}(\mathscr{H}_{c}) $$

such that

- (1) $\mathscr{B}_{c}^{\mathbf{A}^{1}}\simeq\mathscr{J}_{c}$ . (See Proposition 5.2.1)

- (2) The natural $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ action on $\mathscr{B}_{c}$ is strictly compatible with the monoidal structure. (See Proposition 5.2.3)

- (3) $HH(\mathscr{H}_{c};\mathrm{Frob})\simeq HH(\mathscr{B}_{c};\mathrm{Frob})$ . (See Proposition 6.2.1)

Here, $\gr_{0}(1_{c})$ is a certain algebra object in $\mathscr{H}_{c}$ defined in terms of the $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ -action on $\mathscr{H}_{c}$ .

#### 1.2.13.

Unfortunately for the purposes of proving point (3) of the previous paragraph, the category $\mathscr{B}_{c}$ is not quite Morita equivalent to $\mathscr{H}_{c}$ . Nevertheless, if we let

$$ \mathscr{H}_{c}^{\mathrm{access}}=\mathscr{H}_{c}\otimes_{\mathscr{H}_{\leq c}}\mathscr{H}_{\leq c}^{\mathrm{access}} $$

then we show in §4.4 that the natural inclusion $\mathscr{H}_{c}^{\mathrm{access}}\to\mathscr{H}_{c}$ admits a continuous right adjoint, and $\mathscr{H}_{c}^{\mathrm{access}}$ admits a monoidal structure such that this right adjoint is strictly monoidal. In Proposition 5.1.2 we show that the action of $\mathscr{H}_{c}$ on $\gr_{0}(1_{c})\textrm{-mod}(\mathscr{H}_{c})$ factors through $\mathscr{H}_{c}^{\mathrm{access}}$ and $\gr_{0}(1_{c})\textrm{-mod}(\mathscr{H}_{c})$ defines a Morita equivalence between $\mathscr{B}_{c}$ and $\mathscr{H}_{c}^{\mathrm{access}}$ . Finally, in Proposition 6.2.1, using the equivalence

$$ HH(\mathscr{H};\mathrm{Frob})\simeq\Rep(G(\mathbf{F}_{q}))^{\mathrm{unip}} $$

we show that the map

$$ \mathscr{H}_{c}\to\mathscr{H}_{c}^{\mathrm{access}} $$

induces an isomorphism after passing to $HH(-;\mathrm{Frob})$ .

#### 1.2.14.

The final difficulty that arises when trying to implement the argument of §1.2.11 one category level up is that dg categories are much less “rigid” than vector spaces: in general, if the action of $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ on a dg category $\mathscr{C}$ is trivializable on a Zariski dense subset, there’s no reason to expect that the whole action of $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ on $\mathscr{C}$ is trivializable. However, if $\mathscr{C}$ is semisimple and the coaction functor

$$ \mathrm{coact}:\mathscr{C}\to\mathscr{C}\otimes\QCoh(\mathbf{A}^{1}) $$

is strongly continuous (meaning that it admits a continuous right adjoint), it is actually true that the action of $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ on $\mathscr{C}$ is trivializable.

Annoyingly, it is not a priori obvious that the coaction of $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ on $HH(\mathscr{B}_{c};\mathrm{Frob})$ is strongly continuous. However, in Proposition 6.4.4 we show that to prove the triviality of the $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ -action it suffices to show that $HH(\mathscr{B}_{c};\mathrm{Frob})$ is an $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ -equivariant colocalization of a category whose coaction functor is strongly continuous. We then supply the needed colocalization by analyzing a certain renormalization of $\mathscr{B}_{c}$ (see §6.4).

#### 1.2.15.

To summarize our proof of Theorem 1.2.9, we have constructed maps

$$ \mathscr{H}_{c}\textrm{-mod}\xrightarrow{\gr_{0}(1_{c})\textrm{-mod}(\mathscr{H}_{c})\otimes_{\mathscr{H}_{c}}(-)}\mathscr{B}_{c}\textrm{-mod}\xrightarrow{\mathrm{ind}_{\gr_{\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{.5}{$\bullet$}}}}}}}\mathscr{J}_{c}\textrm{-mod} $$

and shown that they induce isomorphisms

$$ HH(\mathscr{H}_{c};\mathrm{Frob})\simeq HH(\mathscr{B}_{c};\mathrm{Frob})\simeq HH(\mathscr{J}_{c};\id) $$

after applying categorical trace. We would like to suggest that the composite map (7) should be viewed as a 2-categorification of Lusztig’s map from the Hecke algebra to the asymptotic algebra (see [Lus87, §2.4], [Cur88, Theorem 9.2]). We remind that the asymptotic algebra $J_{c}$ is $K^{0}(\mathscr{J}_{c})$ . It has a distinguished basis $\left\{j_{w}\right\}$ given by the K-theory classes of the simple objects $J_{w}$ . There is a naive map

$$ \gr_{c}:H\to J_{c}[v^{\pm 1}] $$

of $\mathbf{Z}[v^{\pm 1}]$ -modules which sends

$$ b_{w}\mapsto\begin{cases}j_{w}&w\in c\\
0&w\notin c\end{cases}. $$

This naive map is basically never a ring homomorphism. However, Lusztig observed that if we write

$$ e_{c}=\sum_{d\in\mathscr{D}_{c}}b_{d} $$

where $\mathscr{D}_{c}$ refers to the set of Duflo involutions in the two-sided cell $c$ , then the composite

$$ H\xrightarrow{e_{c}*(-)}H\xrightarrow{\gr_{c}}J_{c}[v^{\pm 1}] $$

is actually a map of rings. In Proposition 4.3.3, we show that

$$ \gr_{0}(1_{c})\simeq\bigoplus_{d\in\mathscr{D}_{c}}L_{d}[-a] $$

so the maps (7) and (8) seem quite clearly related. However, we do not know how to obtain the latter map as a decategorification of the former.

#### 1.2.16. Relationship to [Lus15]

Let’s recall Lusztig’s definition of the partition of irreducible unipotent representations into families indexed by two-sided cells from [Lus79, §8]. If we write $DL_{w}$ for the character of the unipotent Deligne-Lusztig representation corresponding to $w$ , then for any irreducible representation $V$ of $W$ with character $\chi$ , we can define a class function for $G(\mathbf{F}_{q})$ by the formula

$$ DL_{\chi}=\frac{1}{|W|}\sum_{w\in W}\chi(w)DL_{w}. $$

The irreducible representations of $W$ are partitioned into families indexed by two-sided cells as follows: the two-sided cells determine a filtration of the Hecke algebra $H$ by two-sided ideals, and evaluating at $v=1$ gives a filtration of the group algebra of $W$ by two-sided ideals. A representation of $W$ then belongs to the family corresponding to a two-sided cell $c$ if it arises in the isotypic decomposition of the $c$ -graded component of $k[W]$ .33 3 Strictly speaking, families of $W$ -representations are defined in [Lus84, §4.2] somewhat differently, using parabolic induction and generic degrees of $W$ -representations. However, a theorem of Barbasch and Vogan [BV83, Theorem 2.29] (see also [Lus84, Theorem 5.25]) shows that these definitions agree. Lusztig’s disjointness theorem [Lus84, Theorem 6.17] states that if $\rho$ is the character of an irreducible unipotent representation of $G(\mathbf{F}_{q})$ , and $\chi$ , $\chi^{\prime}$ are irreducible characters of $W$ such that

$$ \left\langle\rho,DL_{\chi}\right\rangle\neq 0\quad\text{ and }\quad\left\langle\rho,DL_{\chi^{\prime}}\right\rangle\neq 0 $$

then $\chi$ and $\chi^{\prime}$ belong to the same family. Since [DL76] shows that every unipotent $\rho$ has a nonzero inner product with some $DL_{w}$ , Lusztig partitions the irreducible unipotent representations $\rho$ into families indexed by two-sided cells by stipulating that $\rho$ lies in the family corresponding to $c$ if it has a nonzero pairing with $DL_{\chi}$ for some $\chi$ in $\Rep(W)_{c}$ .

In [Lus15], using this definition of $\Rep(G(\mathbf{F}_{q}))^{\mathrm{unip}}_{c}$ Lusztig shows that

$$ \Rep(G(\mathbf{F}_{q}))^{\mathrm{unip}}_{c}\simeq Z(\mathscr{J}_{c}) $$

where $Z(-)$ refers to the categorical center. To do this, he uses the theory of [Lus84] (most notably [Lus84, Theorem 3.8] and [Lus84, Theorem 6.17]) to show that $\Rep(G(\mathbf{F}_{q}))^{\mathrm{unip}}_{c}$ is monadic over $\mathscr{J}_{c}$ . By the results of [ENO05], $Z(\mathscr{J}_{c})$ is also monadic over $\mathscr{J}_{c}$ , and Lusztig proves (9) by showing that the two monads are isomorphic.

Because $\mathscr{J}_{c}$ is a pivotal, rigid monoidal category (see [EW21, Theorem 5.2]), there is a canonical equivalence

$$ Z(\mathscr{J}_{c})\simeq HH(\mathscr{J}_{c}) $$

(see [BZN15, §3]). We expect, but cannot currently prove that:

- (1) Our definition of $\Rep(G(\mathbf{F}_{q}))^{\mathrm{unip}}_{c}$ agrees with Lusztig’s (perhaps up to replacing $c$ with $w_{0}c$ ).

- (2) With respect to the equivalence (10), our equivalence Theorem 1.2.9 identifies with Lusztig’s equivalence (9).

### 1.3. Future directions

#### 1.3.1. Lusztig’s character formula

It follows from a combination of Proposition 5.1.2, Proposition 5.1.2, and Proposition 5.3.2 that in the diagram

$$ {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{B}_{c}\textrm{-mod}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{H}_{c}\textrm{-mod}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{J}_{c}\textrm{-mod}} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\gr_{0}(1_{c})\textrm{-mod}^{r}(\mathscr{H}_{c})\otimes_{\mathscr{B}_{c}}(-)} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{ind}_{\gr_{\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{.5}{$\scriptstyle\bullet$}}}}}}} $$

all of the objects are 2-dualizable and all of the arrows are 2-adjointable (in the sense of [GRV26]). Moreover, the arrows in the diagram intertwine the pair of commuting endomorphisms $(\id,\mathrm{Frob})$ of $\mathscr{B}_{c}\textrm{-mod}$ with the pairs $(\id,\mathrm{Frob})$ of $\mathscr{H}_{c}\textrm{-mod}$ and $(\id,\id)$ of $\mathscr{J}_{c}\textrm{-mod}$ . It follows that we obtain a commuting diagram

$$ {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\tr(\id;\tr(\mathrm{Frob};\mathscr{H}_{c}\textrm{-mod}))} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\tr(\id;\tr(\mathrm{Frob};\mathscr{B}_{c}\textrm{-mod}))} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\tr(\id;\tr(\id;\mathscr{J}_{c}\textrm{-mod}))} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\tr(\mathrm{Frob};\tr(\id;\mathscr{H}_{c}\textrm{-mod}))} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\tr(\mathrm{Frob};\tr(\id;\mathscr{B}_{c}\textrm{-mod}))} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\tr(\id;\tr(\id;\mathscr{J}_{c}\textrm{-mod}))} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces S} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces S} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces S} $$

where the vertical arrows are the isomorphisms constructed in [BZN13] (see also [GRV26]), and the horizontal arrows in the upper row are isomorphisms by Proposition 6.2.1 and Proposition 6.4.4. By §1.2.9,

$$ \tr(\id;\tr(\id;\mathscr{J}_{c}\textrm{-mod}))\simeq\tr(\id;\tr(\id;\Vect_{A_{c},\omega}\textrm{-mod}))\simeq\Gamma(Z^{(2)}_{A_{c}};\mathscr{L}) $$

where $\mathscr{L}$ is some line bundle depending on $\omega$ and $Z^{(2)}_{A_{c}}$ refers to the “commuting stack” of pairs of commuting elements of $A_{c}$ mod conjugacy. The line bundle $\mathscr{L}$ is known by case-by-case computations to be trivializable, see §6.5.2. With respect to this identification, $S$ acts on $\Gamma(Z^{(2)}_{A_{c}},\mathscr{O})$ via the automorphism of $Z^{(2)}_{A_{c}}$ that swaps the elements in the commuting pair (up to a scalar factor if $\omega\in H^{3}(A_{c};{\mathbf{G}_{m}})$ is nontrivial), see [FQ93]. It should be possible to rederive Lusztig’s character formula from this point of view, as predicted by Ben-Zvi and Nadler (see [BZN13, Remark 1.5]). There are two main difficulties that arise: first, before passing to trace of Frobenius, the arrows

$$ {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\tr(\id;\mathscr{B}_{c}\textrm{-mod})} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\tr(\id;\mathscr{H}_{c}\textrm{-mod})} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\tr(\id;\mathscr{J}_{c}\textrm{-mod})} $$

are not isomorphisms. Second, in the diagram

$$ \mathscr{H}_{\not\leq c}\textrm{-mod}\rightleftarrows\mathscr{H}\textrm{-mod}\rightleftarrows\mathscr{H}_{\leq c}\textrm{-mod} $$

only the rightward arrows are 2-adjointable, so the vector space

$$ \tr(\id;\tr(\mathrm{Frob};\mathscr{H}_{c}\textrm{-mod}))\simeq\tr(\mathrm{Frob};\tr(\id;\mathscr{H}_{c}\textrm{-mod})) $$

is a priori only a subquotient of the space of class functions on $G(\mathbf{F}_{q})$ . We hope to address both of these points in a future publication.

#### 1.3.2. Characterizing $A_{c}$

An unsatisfactory feature of the analysis in this paper is the fact that for us the group $A_{c}$ is defined very inexplicitly. In fact, Losev and Ostrik show [LO14, Theorem 7.4] that the group $A_{c}$ can be completely characterized as follows: in characteristic zero, there is a bijection between two-sided cells and certain nilpotent orbits called special nilpotent orbits. Let $\mathbf{O}$ denote the special nilpotent orbit associated to $c$ , and let $\mathrm{Spr}(\mathbf{O})$ denote the Springer representation attached $\mathbf{O}$ . We can then consider the subrepresentation

$$ \mathrm{Spr}(\mathbf{O})_{c}\subseteq\mathrm{Spr}(\mathbf{O}) $$

consisting of the isotypic components in the family $\Irr(W)_{c}$ corresponding to $c$ ; the group $A_{c}$ can then be characterized as the smallest quotient of the component group $A(\mathbf{O})$ through which the action on $\mathrm{Spr}(\mathbf{O})_{c}$ factors.44 4 The fact that $\Rep(G(\mathbf{F}_{q}))^{\mathrm{unip}}_{c}$ can be described as $\QCoh(A_{c}/A_{c})$ , where $A_{c}$ is defined in terms of Springer theory as above, was already observed in [Lus84, §13.1] prior to the introduction of the asymptotic algebra.

Unfortunately for our goal of finding a uniform account of the theory of unipotent representations, Losev and Ostrik’s characterization of $A_{c}$ relies on many type-by-type calculations. However, recently in the work of G. Dhillon and J. Faergeman [DF25, Theorem 1.10.8.1] the theory of categorical traces has led to simplifications in certain parts of the Losev and Ostrik’s argument. We hope to investigate the theory of the aysmptotic algebra futher from the perspective of $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ actions.

#### 1.3.3. Quasisplit and Suzuki-Ree groups

Although we have restricted for simplicity to the case of split groups, we expect that the results of this paper on the relationship between the Hecke category and the asymptotic category should extend to the cases of quasisplit and Suzuki-Ree groups with only minor adjustments: most importantly, the Steinberg endomorphism of $G$ induces a nontrivial endomorphism $F$ of the asymptotic category. For quasisplit groups, the equivalence

$$ \mathscr{J}_{c}\textrm{-mod}\simeq\Vect_{A_{c}}\textrm{-mod} $$

of §1.2.9 should acquire a natural $F$ -equivariant structure. However, one should not expect this for the Suzuki-Ree groups.

For example, consider the case $G=B_{2}$ with $F$ the endomorphism giving rise to the Suzuki group. If we take

$$ c=\left\{s,t,st,ts,sts,tst\right\} $$

to be the two-sided cell corresponding to the subregular nilpotent orbit, then $F$ acts on $\mathscr{J}_{c}$ by swapping $s$ and $t$ . The group $A_{c}$ is $\mathbf{Z}/2$ , and the category $\mathscr{M}_{c}$ of §1.2.9 is

$$ \mathscr{M}_{c}=\QCoh(Y_{c}), $$

where the $A_{c}$ -set $Y_{c}$ is $\left\{L,M,N\right\}$ . Here the action of $A_{c}$ fixes $L$ and swaps $M$ and $N$ . Under the equivalence

$$ \mathscr{J}_{c}\simeq\QCoh_{A_{c}}(Y_{c}\times Y_{c}) $$

of [BFO09, LO14], the object $J_{s}$ goes to the trivial representation of the stabilizer of $(L,L)$ , while the object $J_{t}$ goes to the constant sheaf on the orbit $\left\{(M,M),(N,N)\right\}$ . It follows that there is no automorphism of $Y_{c}$ which is compatible with the Suzuki endomorphism of $\mathscr{J}_{c}$ with respect to the action of $\mathscr{J}_{c}$ on $\mathscr{M}_{c}$ .

In fact, [Lus84, p. 373, 2nd Table] (see also [Bru06]) shows that the family of unipotent representations of the Suzuki group associated to the cell $c$ has only two elements. In particular, it cannot arise as $\QCoh(\Gamma/\Gamma)$ for any finite group $\Gamma$ .

#### 1.3.4. Other Coxeter groups

Even though the Hecke category $\mathscr{H}$ and the two-sided cell filtration make sense for any Coxeter group $W$ , in this paper we have only investigated the case where $W$ is a finite Weyl group. Let us highlight a few places in our analysis where we expect that the results should generalize to other Coxeter groups, even though our current proof relies on the fact that $W$ is a finite Weyl group. First, our argument that

$$ \tr(\mathrm{Frob};\mathscr{B}_{c}\textrm{-mod})\simeq\tr(\id;\mathscr{J}_{c}\textrm{-mod}) $$

is semisimple relies on the fact that $\tr(\mathrm{Frob};\mathscr{H}_{c}\textrm{-mod})$ is known to be semisimple (via its relationship to $\Rep(G(\mathbf{F}_{q}))$ ), however, we suspect that it is possible to prove the identity (11) for any finite Coxeter group, and deduce semisimplicity as a consequence. A proof along these lines might shed light on the relationship, conjectured in [Lus15, §7.2], between Lusztig’s generalized unipotent characters [Lus93] and $HH(\mathscr{J}_{c})$ .

Additionally, our argument in §5.2 that the action of $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ on $\mathscr{B}_{c}$ is strictly compatible with the monoidal structure seems far from optimal. One could instead try to prove result this by categorifying Lusztig’s proof that the map $\psi_{c}$ is a ring homomorphism. This strategy would presumably involve analyzing the category $\mathscr{H}_{c}^{{\mathbf{G}_{m}}\times{\mathbf{G}_{m}}}$ of bigraded objects, and would hopefully apply to Coxeter groups which are not finite.
