## 2. Semi-rigid monoidal categories

#### 2.0.1.

The goal of this section is to prove some basic facts about semi-rigid monoidal categories which will be useful for us later.

The outline of this section is as follows:

- – In §2.1 we prove a couple of facts about semiorthogonal decompositions of semi-rigid categories.

- – In §2.2 we recall some basic facts from the formalism of categorical traces, and study the relationship between semi-rigidity and the formation of categorical traces.

### 2.1. Semiorthogonal decompositions

#### Proposition 2.1.0.

Suppose that $\mathscr{A}$ is a semi-rigid monoidal category. If

$$ \mathscr{A}_{\ell}\rightleftarrows\mathscr{A}\rightleftarrows\mathscr{A}_{r} $$

is a semiorthogonal decomposition of $\mathscr{A}$ , and if either $\mathscr{A}_{\ell}$ or $\mathscr{A}_{r}$ is a two-sided ideal in $\mathscr{A}$ , then the other category is too, and both $\mathscr{A}_{\ell}$ and $\mathscr{A}_{r}$ admit unique monoidal structures such that $\mathscr{A}\to\mathscr{A}_{\ell}$ and $\mathscr{A}\to\mathscr{A}_{r}$ are monoidal.

#### Proof.

We will consider the case when $\mathscr{A}_{r}$ is a two-sided ideal. The case when $\mathscr{A}_{\ell}$ is a two-sided ideal is completely analogous. Since $\mathscr{A}_{r}$ is a two-sided ideal, it acquires a unique $(\mathscr{A},\mathscr{A})$ -bimodule structure such that the inclusion $\mathscr{A}_{r}\to\mathscr{A}$ is bilinear. It follows that

$$ \mathscr{A}_{\ell}=\cof(\mathscr{A}_{r}\to\mathscr{A}) $$

acquires a unique $(\mathscr{A},\mathscr{A})$ -bimodule structure such that the projection $\mathscr{A}\to\mathscr{A}_{\ell}$ is bilinear. Since $\mathscr{A}$ is semi-rigid, the a priori oplax $(\mathscr{A},\mathscr{A})$ -bilinear structures on the inclusion $\mathscr{A}_{\ell}\to\mathscr{A}$ and the projection $\mathscr{A}\to\mathscr{A}_{r}$ are actually strict.

Because $\mathscr{A}_{\ell}$ is a two-sided ideal in $\mathscr{A}$ , it follows from [Lur17, Proposition 2.2.1.9] (arguing as in [Lur17, Proposition 4.8.2.7]) that $\mathscr{A}_{r}$ admits a unique monoidal structure such that $\mathscr{A}\to\mathscr{A}_{r}$ is monoidal. The same is also true for $\mathscr{A}\to\mathscr{A}_{\ell}$ . ∎

#### Proposition 2.1.0.

Suppose that $\mathscr{A}$ is a semi-rigid monoidal category. If $\mathscr{B}$ is a monoidal localization or colocalization of $\mathscr{A}$ then $\mathscr{B}$ is semi-rigid as well.

#### Proof.

First suppose that $\mathscr{B}$ is a monoidal localization of $\mathscr{A}$ . Because $\mathscr{B}$ is a retract of $\mathscr{A}$ , it is dualizable. It remains to show that

$$ \mathrm{mult}:\mathscr{B}\otimes\mathscr{B}\to\mathscr{B} $$

admits a continuous, $\mathscr{B}$ -bilinear right adjoint. Since $\mathrm{mult}$ is $\mathscr{A}$ -bilinear, if $\mathrm{mult}^{R}$ is continuous then it is automatically $\mathscr{A}$ -bilinear, and hence $\mathscr{B}$ -bilinear. It suffices to check that $\mathrm{mult}^{R}$ is continuous after post-composing with the continuous, conservative functor $i\otimes\id:\mathscr{B}\otimes\mathscr{B}\to\mathscr{A}\otimes\mathscr{B}$ . The left adjoint of the composite functor is

$$ \mathscr{A}\otimes\mathscr{B}\xrightarrow{\pi}\mathscr{B}\otimes\mathscr{B}\xrightarrow{\mathrm{mult}}\mathscr{B} $$

which identifies with the action of $\mathscr{A}$ on $\mathscr{B}$ . Because $\mathscr{A}$ is semi-rigid, this functor automatically has a continuous right adjoint.

Now suppose that $\mathscr{B}$ is a monoidal colocalization of $\mathscr{A}$ . Like in the previous case, it’s enough to show that $\mathrm{mult}:\mathscr{B}\otimes\mathscr{B}\to\mathscr{B}$ admits a continuous right adjoint. However, this functor can be factored as

$$ \mathscr{B}\otimes\mathscr{B}\xrightarrow{i\otimes\id}\mathscr{A}\otimes\mathscr{B}\xrightarrow{\mathrm{act}}\mathscr{B}, $$

and both functors in the composite admit continuous right adjoints. ∎

### 2.2. Traces

#### 2.2.1.

Recall from §1.2.1 that for a monoidal category $\mathscr{A}$ and $(\mathscr{A},\mathscr{A})$ -bimodule $\mathscr{M}$ , the Hochschild homology $HH(\mathscr{A},\mathscr{M})$ is defined to be

$$ HH(\mathscr{A},\mathscr{M})=\mathscr{A}\underset{\mathscr{A}\otimes\mathscr{A}^{\mathrm{rev}}}{\otimes}\mathscr{M}. $$

Recall also that the formalism of categorical traces §1.2.7 allows us to rewrite

$$ HH(\mathscr{A},\mathscr{M})\simeq\tr(\mathscr{M};\mathscr{A}\textrm{-mod}). $$

As a result, the functoriality of categorical traces (see for example [GKRV22]) gives rise to functoriality for $HH$ .

We will be especially interested in the following functoriality of $HH$ : let $\mathscr{A}$ and $\mathscr{B}$ be monoidal categories, and let $f:\mathscr{A}\to\mathscr{B}$ be a monoidal functor between them. Suppose that $\mathscr{A}$ and $\mathscr{B}$ have monoidal endomorphisms $\phi$ and $\psi$ that are intertwined by $f$ . Then the functoriality of categorical traces gives us a map $HH(\mathscr{A};\phi)\to HH(\mathscr{B};\psi)$ , which is the composite

$$ \begin{split}&\mathscr{A}\underset{\mathscr{A}\otimes\mathscr{A}^{\mathrm{rev}}}{\otimes}\mathscr{A}_{\phi}\to\mathscr{B}\underset{\mathscr{A}\otimes\mathscr{A}^{\mathrm{rev}}}{\otimes}\mathscr{A}_{\phi}\simeq\mathscr{B}\underset{\mathscr{B}\otimes\mathscr{B}^{\mathrm{rev}}}{\otimes}\left(\mathscr{B}\underset{\mathscr{A}}{\otimes}\mathscr{A}_{\phi}\underset{\mathscr{A}}{\otimes}\mathscr{B}\right)\\
&\simeq\mathscr{B}\underset{\mathscr{B}\otimes\mathscr{B}^{\mathrm{rev}}}{\otimes}\left(\mathscr{B}_{\psi}\underset{\mathscr{B}}{\otimes}\mathscr{B}\underset{\mathscr{A}}{\otimes}\mathscr{B}\right)\to\mathscr{B}\underset{\mathscr{B}\otimes\mathscr{B}^{\mathrm{rev}}}{\otimes}\left(\mathscr{B}_{\psi}\underset{\mathscr{B}}{\otimes}\mathscr{B}\right)\simeq\mathscr{B}\underset{\mathscr{B}\otimes\mathscr{B}^{\mathrm{rev}}}{\otimes}\mathscr{B}_{\psi}\end{split} $$

where the first non-invertible arrow is obtained by tensoring up from $f:\mathscr{A}\to\mathscr{B}$ , and the second non-invertible arrow is obtained by tensoring up from

$$ \mathrm{mult}:\mathscr{B}\otimes_{\mathscr{A}}\mathscr{B}\to\mathscr{B}. $$

#### 2.2.2.

Because the multiplication functor

$$ \mathrm{mult}:\mathscr{A}\otimes\mathscr{A}\to\mathscr{A} $$

is $(\mathscr{A},\mathscr{A})$ -bilinear, we may tensor this map with $\mathscr{M}$ over $\mathscr{A}\otimes\mathscr{A}^{\mathrm{rev}}$ to obtain a canonical map

$$ \mathscr{M}\to HH(\mathscr{A},\mathscr{M}) $$

called the universal trace. When $\mathscr{A}$ is semi-rigid, $\mathrm{mult}$ admits a continuous $(\mathscr{A},\mathscr{A})$ -bilinear right adjoint, so the universal trace necessarily admits a continuous right adjoint. Additionally, because $\mathrm{mult}$ is generating (because it is after all essentially surjective), it follows that the universal trace is as well. In particular, $HH(\mathscr{A},\mathscr{M})$ is monadic over $\mathscr{M}$ .

#### Construction 2.2.2.

Suppose that $\mathscr{A}$ is a semi-rigid monoidal category and

$$ \mathscr{A}_{\ell}\rightleftarrows\mathscr{A}\rightleftarrows\mathscr{A}_{r} $$

is a semiorthogonal decomposition such that the arrows are all $(\mathscr{A},\mathscr{A})$ -bilinear. Suppose that $\phi$ is a monoidal endomorphism of $\mathscr{A}$ that preserves the given semiorthogonal decomposition. Then there is a commutative diagram

$$ {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\tr(\phi;\mathscr{A}_{\ell}\textrm{-mod})} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\tr(\phi;\mathscr{A}\textrm{-mod})} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\tr(\phi;\mathscr{A}_{r}\textrm{-mod})} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{A}_{\ell}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{A}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{A}_{r}} $$

where the horizontal rows are semiorthogonal decomopositions and the vertical arrows realize the upper categories as monadic over the lower categories.

#### Proof.

Starting with the semiorthogonal decomposition

$$ \mathscr{A}_{\ell}\rightleftarrows\mathscr{A}\rightleftarrows\mathscr{A}_{r} $$

of $(\mathscr{A},\mathscr{A})$ -bimodules, we can twist the action of $\mathscr{A}$ on the right by $\phi$ to obtain a semiorthogonal decomposition

$$ (\mathscr{A}_{\ell})_{\phi}\rightleftarrows\mathscr{A}_{\phi}\rightleftarrows(\mathscr{A}_{r})_{\phi} $$

of $(\mathscr{A},\mathscr{A})$ -bimodules. As in §2.2.2 the adjunction

$$ \mathrm{mult}:\mathscr{A}\otimes\mathscr{A}\rightleftarrows\mathscr{A}:\mathrm{mult}^{R} $$

realizes $\mathscr{A}$ as monadic over $\mathscr{A}\otimes\mathscr{A}$ . Tensoring (12) and (13) over $\mathscr{A}\otimes\mathscr{A}^{\mathrm{rev}}$ gives a diagram

$$ {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(\mathscr{A}_{\ell})_{\phi}\underset{\mathscr{A}\otimes\mathscr{A}^{\mathrm{rev}}}{\otimes}\mathscr{A}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\tr(\phi;\mathscr{A}\textrm{-mod})} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(\mathscr{A}_{r})_{\phi}\underset{\mathscr{A}\otimes\mathscr{A}^{\mathrm{rev}}}{\otimes}\mathscr{A}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{A}_{\ell}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{A}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{A}_{r}} $$

Because the functor $(-)\otimes_{\mathscr{A}\otimes\mathscr{A}^{\mathrm{rev}}}\mathscr{A}$ commutes with colimits,

$$ \cof\left((\mathscr{A}_{\ell})_{\phi}\underset{\mathscr{A}\otimes\mathscr{A}^{\mathrm{rev}}}{\otimes}\mathscr{A}\to\mathscr{A}_{\phi}\underset{\mathscr{A}\otimes\mathscr{A}^{\mathrm{rev}}}{\otimes}\mathscr{A}\right)\simeq\cof((\mathscr{A}_{\ell})_{\phi}\to\mathscr{A}_{\phi})\underset{\mathscr{A}\otimes\mathscr{A}^{\mathrm{rev}}}{\otimes}\mathscr{A}\simeq\mathscr{A}_{r}\underset{\mathscr{A}\otimes\mathscr{A}^{\mathrm{rev}}}{\otimes}\mathscr{A} $$

and it follows that the upper row of (14) is indeed a semiorthogonal decomposition. It remains to identify $(\mathscr{A}_{\ell})_{\phi}\underset{\mathscr{A}\otimes\mathscr{A}^{\mathrm{rev}}}{\otimes}\mathscr{A}$ with $\tr(\phi;\mathscr{A}_{\ell}\textrm{-mod})$ (the proof for $\mathscr{A}_{r}$ is the same). Indeed:

$$ (\mathscr{A}_{\ell})_{\phi}\underset{\mathscr{A}\otimes\mathscr{A}^{\mathrm{rev}}}{\otimes}\mathscr{A}\simeq(\mathscr{A}_{\ell})_{\phi}\underset{\mathscr{A}_{\ell}\otimes\mathscr{A}_{\ell}^{\mathrm{rev}}}{\otimes}\mathscr{A}_{\ell}\otimes\mathscr{A}_{\ell}\underset{\mathscr{A}\otimes\mathscr{A}^{\mathrm{rev}}}{\otimes}\mathscr{A}\simeq(\mathscr{A}_{\ell})_{\phi}\underset{\mathscr{A}_{\ell}\otimes\mathscr{A}_{\ell}^{\mathrm{rev}}}{\otimes}\mathscr{A}_{\ell}\underset{\mathscr{A}}{\otimes}\mathscr{A}_{\ell} $$

and the result follows because $\mathscr{A}_{\ell}\otimes_{\mathscr{A}}\mathscr{A}_{\ell}\simeq\mathscr{A}_{\ell}$ as an $(\mathscr{A}_{\ell},\mathscr{A}_{\ell})$ -bimodule. ∎

#### Proposition 2.2.2.

The map

$$ HH(\mathscr{A};\phi)\to HH(\mathscr{A}_{\ell};\phi) $$

of Construction 2.2.2 identifies with the map from §2.2.1.

#### Proof.

Unwinding the definition of the functoriality of $HH$ shows that the map

$$ HH(\mathscr{A};\phi)\to HH(\mathscr{A}_{\ell};\phi) $$

identifies with the composite

$$ \mathscr{A}_{\phi}\underset{\mathscr{A}\otimes\mathscr{A}^{\mathrm{rev}}}{\otimes}\mathscr{A}\to\mathscr{A}_{\phi}\underset{\mathscr{A}\otimes\mathscr{A}^{\mathrm{rev}}}{\otimes}\mathscr{A}_{\ell}\xrightarrow{\sim}(\mathscr{A}_{\ell})_{\phi}\underset{\mathscr{A}_{\ell}\otimes\mathscr{A}_{\ell}^{\mathrm{rev}}}{\otimes}\mathscr{A}_{\ell} $$

where the second arrow is a certain isomorphism. In particular, both the map coming from the functoriality of $HH$ and the map of Construction 2.2.2 admit fully faithful left adjoints. Therefore, to prove that the maps are isomorphic it suffices to show that

$$ \mathscr{A}_{\phi}\underset{\mathscr{A}\otimes\mathscr{A}^{\mathrm{rev}}}{\otimes}\mathscr{A}_{\ell}\quad\text{and}\quad(\mathscr{A}_{\ell})_{\phi}\underset{\mathscr{A}\otimes\mathscr{A}^{\mathrm{rev}}}{\otimes}\mathscr{A} $$

agree as full subcategories of $HH(\mathscr{A};\phi)$ . This follows because both subcategories are equal to

$$ (\mathscr{A}_{\ell})_{\phi}\underset{\mathscr{A}\otimes\mathscr{A}^{\mathrm{rev}}}{\otimes}\mathscr{A}_{\ell}. $$

∎

#### 2.2.3.

The analogoue of Proposition 2.2.2 for $\mathscr{A}_{r}$ is true as well, and the proof is the same.

## 3. $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ -actions

#### 3.0.1.

In [GLR26, §1], D. Gaitsgory, K. Lin, and the author proved the following result about actions of the commutative monoid $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ (with the monoid structure given by multiplication) on dg categories:

#### Proposition 3.0.1 ([GLR26, Theorem 1.1.7]).

Suppose that $\mathscr{C}$ is a category acted on by ${\mathbf{G}_{m}}$ . Then the following data are equivalent:

- (1) An extension of the given ${\mathbf{G}_{m}}$ action to an action of $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ .

- (2) A collection of colocalizations $\left\{\mathscr{C}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}_{\leq n}\right\}$ of $\mathscr{C}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}$ such that

$$ \mathscr{C}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}=\colim_{n}\mathscr{C}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}_{\leq n} $$

and $\mathscr{O}(m)\cdot\mathscr{C}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}_{\leq n}=\mathscr{C}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}_{\leq n+m}$ (here $\mathscr{O}(m)$ denote the weight $m$ representation of ${\mathbf{G}_{m}}$ ).

Additionally, if we write $\mathscr{C}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}_{>n}$ for the right orthogonal of $\mathscr{C}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}_{\leq n}$ , then for two categories $\mathscr{C}$ , $\mathscr{D}$ acted on by $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ , an $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ -equivariant functor $F:\mathscr{C}\to\mathscr{D}$ is the same as a $\Rep({\mathbf{G}_{m}})$ -linear functor $F^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}:\mathscr{C}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}\to\mathscr{D}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}$ such that $\mathscr{C}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}_{\leq 0}$ maps to $\mathscr{D}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}_{\leq 0}$ and $\mathscr{C}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}_{>0}$ maps to $\mathscr{D}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}_{>0}$ .

#### 3.0.2.

The goal of this section is to prove a few more results about actions of $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ on dg categories which will be useful to us. Many of these results are based on conversations with K. Lin.

The outline of this section is as follows:

- – In §3.1 we give a simple criterion to recognize when a category $\mathscr{D}$ is the category of $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ -invariants for a category $\mathscr{C}$ acted on by $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ .

- – In §3.2 we study the interaction of $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ -actions with the formation of Hochschild homology.

- – In §3.3 we give a characterization of when a functor between categories acted on by $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ admits a left- or right-lax $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ -equivariant structure.

- – In §3.4 we study $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ actions on categories which are monadic over a category with a preexisting action of $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ .

### 3.1. Invariants

#### 3.1.1.

Let $\mathscr{C}$ be a category acted on by $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ . The goal of this section is to prove a simple characterization of the category of $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ -invariants $\mathscr{C}^{\mathbf{A}^{1}}$ . First we note that because

$$ 0\cdot\lambda=\lambda\cdot 0=0 $$

for all $\lambda\in\mathbf{A}^{1}$ , the map

$$ \mathrm{act}_{0}:\mathscr{C}\to\mathscr{C} $$

naturally intertwines the trivial $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ -action on the source with the given $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ -action on the target, and it intertwines the given $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ -action on the source with the trivial $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ -action on the target. In particular, by the universal property of the category of invariants, there is a unique map $r:\mathscr{C}\to\mathscr{C}^{\mathbf{A}^{1}}$ making the diagram

$$ {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{C}^{\mathbf{A}^{1}}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{C}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{C}} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces i} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{act}_{0}} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces r} $$

commute, where $i:\mathscr{C}^{\mathbf{A}^{1}}\to\mathscr{C}$ is the canonical map.

#### Proposition 3.1.1.

The maps $i$ and $r$ realize $\mathscr{C}^{\mathbf{A}^{1}}$ as the “subobject” of $\mathscr{C}$ corresponding to the idempotent endomorphism $\mathrm{act}_{0}$ of $\mathscr{C}$ .

#### Proof.

Since $i\circ r\simeq\mathrm{act}_{0}$ , it remains to show that $r\circ i\simeq\id_{\mathscr{C}^{\mathbf{A}^{1}}}$ . By the universal property of $\mathscr{C}^{\mathbf{A}^{1}}$ , it suffices to show that

$$ iri\simeq i $$

as $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ -equivariant maps from $\mathscr{C}^{\mathbf{A}^{1}}$ to $\mathscr{C}$ . This follows from the commutativity of the square

$$ {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(\mathscr{C}^{\mathbf{A}^{1}})^{\mathrm{triv}}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{C}^{\mathbf{A}^{1}}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{C}^{\mathrm{triv}}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{C}} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{act}_{0}} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces i} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces i} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{act}_{0}} $$

and the fact that, because the $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ -action on $\mathscr{C}^{\mathbf{A}^{1}}$ is already trivial, the map

$$ \mathrm{act}_{0}:(\mathscr{C}^{\mathbf{A}^{1}})^{\mathrm{triv}}\to\mathscr{C}^{\mathbf{A}^{1}} $$

is isomorphic to the identity. ∎

#### Corollary 3.1.1.

Suppose that $\mathscr{C}$ is a category acted on by $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ . Suppose that we are given a category $\mathscr{D}$ and morphisms $i:\mathscr{D}\to\mathscr{C}$ , $r:\mathscr{C}\to\mathscr{D}$ such that the following diagrams commute

$$ {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{D}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{C}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{C}} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces i} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{act}_{0}} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces r} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{D}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{D}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{C}} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces i} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\id_{\mathscr{D}}} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces r} $$

Then $\mathscr{D}$ is equivalent to $\mathscr{C}^{\mathbf{A}^{1}}$ .

#### Proof.

Follows immediately from Proposition 3.1.1 the uniqueness of “subobjects” corresponding to idempotents. ∎

#### 3.1.2.

As a final remark, let’s note that $r:\mathscr{C}\to\mathscr{C}^{\mathbf{A}^{1}}$ has a natural $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ -equivariance data, where the source has the given $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ action. This is because $r$ is isomorphic to $r\circ\mathrm{act}_{0}$ , and we can write the latter as a composite of $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ -equivariant functors as follows:

$$ \mathscr{C}\xrightarrow{\mathrm{act}_{0}}\mathscr{C}^{\mathrm{triv}}\xrightarrow{r}\mathscr{C}^{\mathbf{A}^{1}}. $$

### 3.2. Hochschild homology

#### 3.2.1.

Let’s start by noting that one can perform the constructions of §2.2.1 internally to a general symmetric monoidal category $\mathscr{C}$ . (The material in §2.2.1 concerns the case when $\mathscr{C}=\mathrm{dgCat}$ ). Namely, an for associative algebra object $A\in\mathscr{C}$ , one can form $HH(A)\in\mathscr{C}$ , which is the object

$$ A\underset{A\otimes A^{\mathrm{rev}}}{\otimes}A. $$

More generally, if $A$ admits an algebra endomorphism $\phi$ , one can form the twisted Hochschild homology

$$ HH(A;\phi)=A\underset{A\otimes A^{\mathrm{rev}}}{\otimes}A_{\phi}. $$

Aditionally, if $A$ and $B$ are algebra objects with endomorphisms and $f:A\to B$ is a map of algebras which intertwines these endomorphisms, then we obtain a map

$$ HH(A;\phi_{A})\xrightarrow{HH(f)}HH(B;\phi_{B}). $$

Applying this paradigm to the situation where $\mathscr{C}=\mathbf{A}^{1}\textrm{-Cat}$ , the symmetric monoidal category of categories acted on by $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ , we see that if $\mathscr{A}$ is an $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ -equivariantly monoidal category and $\phi$ is an $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ -equivariant monoidal automorphism of $\mathscr{A}$ , then the category $HH(\mathscr{A};\phi)$ acquires a natural $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ -action. Concretely, for $\lambda\in\mathbf{A}^{1}$ , the endomorphism $\mathrm{act}_{\lambda}$ of $HH(\mathscr{A};\phi)$ identifies with

$$ HH(\mathrm{act}_{\lambda}):HH(\mathscr{A};\phi)\to HH(\mathscr{A};\phi). $$

#### Proposition 3.2.1.

In the above setup, the action of $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ on $HH(\mathscr{A};\phi)$ has the property that

$$ HH(\mathscr{A};\phi)^{\mathbf{A}^{1}}\simeq HH(\mathscr{A}^{\mathbf{A}^{1}};\phi). $$

#### Proof.

Follows from Corollary 3.1.1 by applying $HH(-)$ to the triangles

$$ {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{A}^{\mathbf{A}^{1}}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{A}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{A}} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces i} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{act}_{0}} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces r} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{A}^{\mathbf{A}^{1}}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{A}^{\mathbf{A}^{1}}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{A}} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces i} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\id_{\mathscr{D}}} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces r} $$

∎

#### Proposition 3.2.1.

In the setup above, if $\mathscr{A}$ is semi-rigid and the $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ action on $\mathscr{A}$ has the property that

$$ \mathrm{coact}:\mathscr{A}\to\mathscr{A}\otimes\QCoh(\mathbf{A}^{1}) $$

admits a continuous right adjoint, then the same is true for the action of $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ on $HH(\mathscr{A};\phi)$ .

#### Proof.

Recall from §2.2.2 that $HH(\mathscr{A};\phi)$ is monadic over $\mathscr{A}$ , so we may check that $\mathrm{coact}^{R}$ is continuous after applying $\mathrm{oblv}:HH(\mathscr{A};\phi)\to\mathscr{A}$ . Now the result follows from the commutativity of

$$ {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces HH(\mathscr{A};\phi)} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces HH(\mathscr{A};\phi)\otimes\QCoh(\mathbf{A}^{1})} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{A}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{A}\otimes\QCoh(\mathbf{A}^{1})} $$

by passing to right adjoints. ∎

### 3.3. Lax equivariance

#### 3.3.1.

Let $\mathscr{C}$ and $\mathscr{D}$ be categories acted on by $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ . We will say that a map $F:\mathscr{C}\to\mathscr{D}$ has a left-lax (resp. right-lax) $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ -equivaraint structure if $F$ has the structure of a left-lax (resp. right-lax) linear map of $\QCoh(\mathbf{A}^{1})$ -modules.

#### Proposition 3.3.1.

Suppose that $F:\mathscr{C}\to\mathscr{D}$ is left-lax $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ -equivariant. Then the image of $\mathscr{C}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}_{\leq n}$ under $F^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}$ is contained in $\mathscr{D}_{\leq n}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}$ .

#### Proof.

Under the equivalence of Proposition 3.0.1, the category $\mathscr{C}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}_{\leq n}$ identifies with

$$ \mathscr{O}(n)\textrm{-comod}(\mathscr{C}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}) $$

where $\mathscr{O}(n)\in\QCoh(\mathbf{A}^{1}/{\mathbf{G}_{m}})$ corresponds under the equivalence $\QCoh(\mathbf{A}^{1}/{\mathbf{G}_{m}})\simeq\Vect^{\mathrm{Fil}}$ with the filtered vector space $V_{\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{.5}{$\bullet$}}}}}$ with

$$ V_{i}=\begin{cases}k&i\geq-n\\
0&\text{otherwise}\end{cases} $$

Since the functor $\mathscr{C}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}\to\mathscr{D}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}$ is assumed to be left-lax $\QCoh(\mathbf{A}^{1}/{\mathbf{G}_{m}})$ -linear, it induces a functor

$$ \mathscr{O}(n)\textrm{-comod}(\mathscr{C}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}})\to\mathscr{O}(n)\textrm{-comod}(\mathscr{D}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}) $$

which is what we wanted to show. ∎

#### Construction 3.3.1.

Suppose $\mathscr{C}$ and $\mathscr{D}$ are categories acted on by $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ and suppose that $F:\mathscr{C}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}\to\mathscr{D}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}$ has the property that $F^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}:\mathscr{C}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}\to\mathscr{D}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}$ sends $\mathscr{C}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}_{\leq n}$ to $\mathscr{D}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}_{\leq n}$ . Then $F$ admits a structure of left-lax $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ -equivariance.

#### Proof.

Consider the comma category $\mathscr{D}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}_{F^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}/-}$ , viewed as a $\Rep({\mathbf{G}_{m}})$ -module category. The objects of $\mathscr{D}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}_{F^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}/-}$ consist of triples $(x,y,\alpha)$ , where $x\in\mathscr{C}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}$ , $y\in\mathscr{D}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}$ , and $\alpha$ is a map $F^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}(x)\to y$ . This category comes equipped with continuous and jointly conservative functors

$$ \begin{split}\mathscr{D}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}_{F^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}/-}\to\mathscr{C}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}\\
\mathscr{D}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}_{F^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}/-}\to\mathscr{D}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}\end{split} $$

sending a triple $(x,y,\alpha)$ to $x$ and $y$ , respectively.

If we set $\mathscr{D}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}_{F^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}/-,\leq 0}$ to be the full subcategory of $\mathscr{D}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}_{F^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}/-}$ consisting of triples $(x,y,\alpha)$ such that $x\in\mathscr{C}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}_{\leq 0}$ and $y\in\mathscr{D}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}_{\leq 0}$ , then we claim that the inclusion

$$ \mathscr{D}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}_{F^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}/-,\leq 0}\to\mathscr{D}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}_{F^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}/-} $$

admits a continuous right adjoint. This right adjoint sends a triple $(x,y,\alpha)$ to the triple $(\tau_{\leq 0}x,\tau_{\leq 0}y,\alpha_{\leq 0})$ , where

$$ \alpha_{\leq 0}:F\tau_{\leq 0}x\to\tau_{\leq 0}y $$

is the map obtained by adjunction from

$$ F\tau_{\leq 0}x\to Fx\xrightarrow{\alpha}y $$

using the fact that $F$ sends $\mathscr{C}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}_{\leq 0}$ to $\mathscr{D}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}_{\leq 0}$ . Note that the continuity of this right adjoint can be checked after applying the functors (15), where it follows from the continuity of the weight truncation functors for $\mathscr{C}$ and $\mathscr{D}$ .

This choice of $\mathscr{D}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}_{F^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}/-,\leq 0}$ defines an $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ action on the de-equivariantization of $\mathscr{D}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}_{F^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}/-}$ , and it has the feature that the forgetful functors to $\mathscr{C}$ and $\mathscr{D}$ are $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ -equivariant (using the criterion for $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ equivariance from Proposition 3.0.1). Now we note that the projection onto the first factor of (15) admits a left adjoint, which sends $x\in\mathscr{C}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}$ to $(x,F^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}x,\id_{F^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}x})$ , and the composite of this left adjoint with the projection onto the second factor identifies with $F^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}$ . As a composition of left-lax $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ equivariant morphisms, $F$ acquires the structure of left-lax $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ -equivariance. ∎

#### 3.3.2.

Proposition 3.3.1 and Construction 3.3.1 show that the essential image of the forgetful functor

$$ \Hom_{\mathbf{A}^{1}\textrm{-left-lax}}(\mathscr{C},\mathscr{D})\to\Hom_{{\mathbf{G}_{m}}}(\mathscr{C},\mathscr{D}) $$

consists of the functors sending $\mathscr{C}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}_{\leq n}$ to $\mathscr{D}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}_{\leq n}$ . More precisely, if we let

$$ \Hom_{{\mathbf{G}_{m}}}(\mathscr{C},\mathscr{D})_{\leq 0} $$

denote the subcategory of $\Hom_{{\mathbf{G}_{m}}}(\mathscr{C},\mathscr{D})$ consisting of functors that send $\mathscr{C}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}_{\leq n}$ to $\mathscr{D}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}_{\leq n}$ , then we have constructed a section of the forgetful functor

$$ \Hom_{\mathbf{A}^{1}\textrm{-left-lax}}(\mathscr{C},\mathscr{D})\to\Hom_{{\mathbf{G}_{m}}}(\mathscr{C},\mathscr{D})_{\leq 0}. $$

We expect that (16) is actually an equivalence. We are unable to show this because we can’t show that if $F:\mathscr{C}\to\mathscr{D}$ is already left-lax $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ -equivariant, then the left-lax $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ -equivariance structure on $F$ constructed in Construction 3.3.1 agrees with the preexisting lax equivariance structure on $F$ .

Let’s note that if one could show a priori that (16) were fully faithful, then it would automatically be an equivalence. Alternatively, one could show that left-lax equivariance structures on $F$ upgrading a given ${\mathbf{G}_{m}}$ -equivariance data are equivalent to $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ -actions on the comma category $\mathscr{D}_{F/-}$ which upgrade the given ${\mathbf{G}_{m}}$ action and have the property that the projections onto $\mathscr{C}$ and $\mathscr{D}$ are $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ -equivariant. In fact, we expect that this should follow from a homotopy coherent version of [Bou14]. (This paper was the inspiration for our Construction 3.3.1.)

#### 3.3.3.

A similar argument to the above shows that right-lax $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ -equivariant functors send $\mathscr{C}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}_{\geq n}$ to $\mathscr{D}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}_{\geq n}$ , and every functor with this property admits the structure of right-lax $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ -equivariance. It follows that every functor $\mathscr{C}\to\mathscr{D}$ which is both left-lax $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ -equivariant and right-lax $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ -equivariant is actually $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ -equivariant.

### 3.4. Monads

#### 3.4.1.

Suppose that $\mathscr{C}$ is a category acted on by $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ , and suppose that $T$ is a ${\mathbf{G}_{m}}$ -equivariant monad on $\mathscr{C}$ . Then the functor

$$ \mathscr{C}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}_{\leq 0}\to\mathscr{C}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}\xrightarrow{\mathrm{ind}}T^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}\textrm{-mod}(\mathscr{C}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}) $$

admits a continuous right adjoint, and so factors uniquely as

$$ \mathscr{C}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}_{\leq 0}\to T^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}\textrm{-mod}(\mathscr{C}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}})_{\leq 0}\hookrightarrow T^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}\textrm{-mod}(\mathscr{C}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}) $$

where the first arrow is generating, the second arrow is fully-faithful, and both arrows have continuous right adjoints. More explicitly, $T^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}\textrm{-mod}(\mathscr{C}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}})_{\leq 0}$ is the full subcategory of $T^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}\textrm{-mod}(\mathscr{C}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}})$ generated by the image of (17).

We claim that under the equivalence of Proposition 3.0.1, $T^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}\textrm{-mod}(\mathscr{C}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}})_{\leq 0}$ specifies an $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ -action on $T\textrm{-mod}(\mathscr{C})$ . Since the inclusion of this subcategory into $T^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}\textrm{-mod}(\mathscr{C}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}})$ has a continuous right adjoint by construction, it just remains to see that

$$ T^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}\textrm{-mod}(\mathscr{C}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}})\simeq\colim_{n}T^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}\textrm{-mod}(\mathscr{C}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}})_{\leq n}. $$

But this follows from the fact that $\mathrm{ind}:\mathscr{C}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}\to T^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}\textrm{-mod}(\mathscr{C}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}})$ is generating and $\mathscr{C}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}$ is generated by $\mathscr{C}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}_{\leq n}$ .

For this $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ -action on $T\textrm{-mod}(\mathscr{C})$ , the functor $\mathrm{ind}:\mathscr{C}\to T\textrm{-mod}(\mathscr{C})$ is tautologically left-lax $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ -equivariant (and hence $\mathrm{oblv}:T\textrm{-mod}(\mathscr{C})\to\mathscr{C}$ is right-lax $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ -equivariant). In some sense, this $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ -action is the minimal action with this property.

#### Proposition 3.4.1.

In the setup of the preceding paragraph, suppose that $T$ is left-lax $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ -equivariant. Then the $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ -action specified above is the unique action on $T\textrm{-mod}(\mathscr{C})$ such that

$$ \mathrm{oblv}:T\textrm{-mod}(\mathscr{C})\to\mathscr{C} $$

is $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ -equivariant. For this $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ -action, the category of invariants $T\textrm{-mod}(\mathscr{C})^{\mathbf{A}^{1}}$ is monadic over $\mathscr{C}^{\mathbf{A}^{1}}$ , and the monad is $\tau_{\geq 0}T^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}$ .

#### Proof.

The uniqueness of such an $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ action is clear: for $\mathrm{oblv}$ to be left-lax $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ -equivariant, it must be the case that

$$ T^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}\textrm{-mod}(\mathscr{C}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}})_{\leq 0}\subseteq T^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}\textrm{-mod}(\mathscr{C}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}})\underset{\mathscr{C}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}}{\times}\mathscr{C}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}_{\leq 0}. $$

Conversely, if $x\in T^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}\textrm{-mod}(\mathscr{C}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}})$ has the proerty that $\mathrm{oblv}(x)\in\mathscr{C}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}_{\leq 0}$ , then

$$ \mathrm{oblv}(\tau_{>0}x)=\tau_{>0}\mathrm{oblv}(x)=0 $$

so $\tau_{>0}x=0$ .

To see that the $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ -action specified above has the property that $\mathrm{oblv}$ is $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ -equivariant, first note that by construction $\mathrm{ind}:\mathscr{C}\to T\textrm{-mod}(\mathscr{C})$ is left-lax $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ -equivariant, and hence $\mathrm{oblv}:T\textrm{-mod}(\mathscr{C})\to\mathscr{C}$ is right-lax $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ -equivariant (this doesn’t use the assumption that $T$ is left-lax $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ -equivariant). It remains to check that $\mathrm{oblv}$ is left-lax $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ -equivariant. We can check on generators whether the image of $T^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}\textrm{-mod}(\mathscr{C}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}})_{\leq 0}$ under $\mathrm{oblv}$ is contained in $\mathscr{C}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}_{\leq 0}$ , and this follows by the assumption that $T$ is left-lax $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ -equivariant.

It remains to characterize the category of invariants for this $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ -action. By our assumption on $T$ , we have a commutative diagram

$$ {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces T^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}\textrm{-mod}(\mathscr{C}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}})_{\leq-1}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces T^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}\textrm{-mod}(\mathscr{C}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}})_{\leq 0}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{C}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}_{\leq-1}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{C}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}_{\leq 0}} $$

which specifies an adjunction in $\mathrm{dgCat}^{\Delta^{1}}$ . Applying the 2-functor

$$ \cof(-):\mathrm{dgCat}^{\Delta^{1}}\to\mathrm{dgCat} $$

we obtain an adjunction

$$ \mathrm{ind}:\mathscr{C}^{\mathbf{A}^{1}}\rightleftarrows T\textrm{-mod}(\mathscr{C})^{\mathbf{A}^{1}}:\mathrm{oblv} $$

which fits into the commutative diagram

$$ {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces T^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}\textrm{-mod}(\mathscr{C}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}})_{\leq-1}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces T^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}\textrm{-mod}(\mathscr{C}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}})_{\leq 0}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces T\textrm{-mod}(\mathscr{C})^{\mathbf{A}^{1}}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{C}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}_{\leq-1}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{C}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}_{\leq 0}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathscr{C}^{\mathbf{A}^{1}}} $$

It is easy to see that the functor we have called $\mathrm{ind}$ is generating by precomposing with the quotient map $\mathscr{C}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}_{\leq 0}\to\mathscr{C}^{\mathbf{A}^{1}}$ , so it follows that $T\textrm{-mod}(\mathscr{C})^{\mathbf{A}^{1}}$ is monadic over $\mathscr{C}^{\mathbf{A}^{1}}$ . By construction, the monad $\mathrm{oblv}\circ\mathrm{ind}$ is the monad on the quotient $\mathscr{C}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}_{\leq 0}/\mathscr{C}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}_{\leq-1}$ induced by $T^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}$ , which shows that it is $\tau_{\geq 0}T^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}$ . ∎

## 4. Analysis of the Hecke category

#### 4.0.1.

The goal of this section is to construct the semiorthogonal decomposition of $\mathscr{H}$ by cells, and show that the associated graded pieces admit $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ -actions whose categories of $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ -invariants recover the asymptotic category $\mathscr{J}_{c}$ .

The outline of this section is as follows:

- – In §4.1 we construct our desired semiorthogonal decomposition of $\mathscr{H}$ by two-sided cells.

- – In §4.2 we show that the theory of weights equips the associated graded pieces $\mathscr{H}_{c}$ of the semiorthogonal decompositions with an $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ -action, and that this action is “left-compatible” with the monoidal structure on $\mathscr{H}_{c}$ .

- – In §4.3 we show that the category $\mathscr{H}_{c}^{\mathbf{A}^{1}}$ identifies with the asymptotic category $\mathscr{J}_{c}$ .

- – In §4.4 we study a variant of the subquotient category which will be useful in later sections.

### 4.1. A semiorthogonal decomposition indexed by cells

#### 4.1.1.

Let $\mathscr{O}_{0}$ denote $\Sh(N\backslash G/B)$ . This is the $\ell$ -adic version of the unbounded derived category of the ind-completion of the principal block of the BGG category $\mathscr{O}$ . For $w\in W$ , let $L_{w}$ denote the IC sheaf of the Schubert variety $X_{w}$ and let $P_{w}$ denote the indecomposable projective cover of $L_{w}$ .

For $S$ a subset of $W$ , let $(\mathscr{O}_{0})_{S}$ denote the full subcategory of $\mathscr{O}_{0}$ consisting of objects with the property that the composition factors of all of their perverse cohomology groups are of the form $L_{w}$ for $w\in S$ . Let $(\mathscr{O}_{0})^{S}$ denote the full subcategory of $\mathscr{O}_{0}$ generated under colimits and shifts by $P_{w}$ for $w\notin S$ .

#### Proposition 4.1.1.

The inclusion of $(\mathscr{O}_{0})_{S}$ admits a left adjoint, the inclusion of $(\mathscr{O}_{0})^{S}$ admits a continuous right adjoint, and

$$ (\mathscr{O}_{0})^{S}\rightleftarrows\mathscr{O}_{0}\rightleftarrows(\mathscr{O}_{0})_{S} $$

is a semiorthogonal decomposition of $\mathscr{O}_{0}$ .

#### Proof.

Because $(\mathscr{O}_{0})^{S}$ is generated by objects which are compact in $\mathscr{O}_{0}$ , it’s clear that the inclusion $(\mathscr{O}_{0})^{S}\to\mathscr{O}_{0}$ admits a continuous right adjoint. It remains to identify the right orthogonal $(\mathscr{O}_{0})^{S,\perp}$ with $(\mathscr{O}_{0})_{S}$ . Because $P_{w}$ is projective, the mapping spectrum

$$ \Hom_{\mathscr{O}_{0}}(P_{w},\mathscr{F}) $$

vanishes if and only if

$$ \Hom_{\mathscr{O}_{0}^{\heartsuit}}(P_{w},H^{p}_{i}(\mathscr{F})) $$

vanishes for all $i$ . Now the result follows from the well-known fact that

$$ \dim\Hom_{\mathscr{O}_{0}^{\heartsuit}}(P_{w},x)=[x:L_{w}]. $$

∎

#### 4.1.2. Example

Let’s consider the case when $G=SL_{2}$ and we take $S=\left\{s\right\}\subseteq W$ . In this case $(\mathscr{O}_{0})^{S}$ is the subcategory generated by the big projective $P_{1}$ . This category is equivalent to the category of modules for $R=\End(P_{1})$ (this ring is commutative). In terms of this description of $(\mathscr{O}_{0})^{S}$ , the inclusion

$$ (\mathscr{O}_{0})^{S}\to\mathscr{O}_{0} $$

identifies with the left adjoint of Soergel’s $\mathbf{V}$ -functor.

Explicitly, $R=k[x]/x^{2}$ . Let $k$ denote the $R$ module where $x$ acts by zero. Let’s calculate $H_{*}(\mathbf{V}^{L}(k))$ . Because $\mathbf{V}$ is t-exact, we know that $\mathbf{V}^{L}$ is right t-exact. We know that

$$ k\simeq\coker(R\xrightarrow{\cdot x}R)\text{ in }R\textrm{-mod}^{\heartsuit} $$

so it follows that

$$ H_{0}(\mathbf{V}^{L}(k))\simeq\coker(P_{1}\xrightarrow{x}P_{1})\simeq\nabla_{s}. $$

From the exact triangle

$$ k\to R\to k $$

in $R\textrm{-mod}$ we obtain an exact triangle

$$ \mathbf{V}^{L}(k)\to P_{1}\to\mathbf{V}^{L}(k) $$

in $\mathscr{O}_{0}$ . In particular, we have an exact sequence

$$ 0=H_{1}(P_{1})\to H_{1}(\mathbf{V}^{L}(k))\to\nabla_{s}\to P_{1}\to\nabla_{s}\to 0 $$

so we calculate that $H_{1}(\mathbf{V}^{L}(k))\simeq L_{s}$ . For all $i\geq 1$ we have an exact sequence

$$ 0=H_{i+1}(P_{1})\to H_{i+1}(\mathbf{V}^{L}(k))\to H_{i}(\mathbf{V}^{L}(k))\to H_{i}(P_{1})=0, $$

so it follows that

$$ H_{i}(\mathbf{V}^{L}(k))\simeq\begin{cases}L_{s}&i>0\\
\nabla_{s}&i=0\\
0&i<0\end{cases} $$

Using this calculation, one can compute the projections $\tau_{S}(x)$ and $\tau^{S}(x)$ for the various indecomposable objects of $\mathscr{O}_{0}$ . As an illustrative example, let’s consider the case $x=L_{1}$ . Then

$$ \tau^{S}(x)\simeq\mathbf{V}^{L}\mathbf{V}(x)\simeq\mathbf{V}^{L}(k) $$

whose homology groups we have already computed. Since

$$ \tau_{S}(x)\simeq\cof(\tau^{S}(x)\to x), $$

we learn that

$$ H_{i}(\tau_{S}(x))\simeq\begin{cases}L_{s}&i\geq 1\\
0&i<1\end{cases} $$

#### 4.1.3.

Let $\mathscr{H}$ denote the equivariant Hecke category $\Sh(B\backslash G/B)$ . In [BZN15, Theorem 1.8.1] it was shown that $\mathscr{H}$ is a pivotal semi-rigid monoidal category. Let

$$ \pi:N\backslash G/B\to B\backslash G/B $$

denote the natural projection. The IC sheaf $L_{w}$ has the property of being $T$ -equivariant (as an object of the abelian category $\mathscr{O}_{0}^{\heartsuit}$ ), and we will abuse notation by using the same symbol $L_{w}$ to denote the corresponding object $L_{w}\in\Sh(B\backslash G/B)$ .

Like in the case of $\mathscr{O}_{0}$ , given a subset $S\subseteq W$ , define $\mathscr{H}_{S}$ to be the subcategory of $\mathscr{H}$ consisting of objects, all of whose perverse cohomologies are filtered colimits of extensions of $L_{w}$ for $w\in S$ , and define $\mathscr{H}^{S}$ to be the subcategory of $\mathscr{H}$ generated by $\pi_{!}P_{w}$ for $w\notin S$ .

#### Proposition 4.1.3.

The inclusion $\mathscr{H}^{S}\to\mathscr{H}$ admits a continuous right adjoint, $\mathscr{H}_{S}\to\mathscr{H}$ admits a continuous left adjoint, and

$$ \mathscr{H}^{S}\rightleftarrows\mathscr{H}\rightleftarrows\mathscr{H}_{S} $$

is a semiorthogonal decomposition of $\mathscr{H}$ . Additionally, $\pi^{!}:\mathscr{H}\to\mathscr{O}_{0}$ sends $\mathscr{H}_{S}$ to $(\mathscr{O}_{0})_{S}$ and $\mathscr{H}^{S}$ to $(\mathscr{O}_{0})^{S}$ .

#### Proof.

As before, the inclusion $\mathscr{H}^{S}\to\mathscr{H}$ admits a continuous right adjoint because $\mathscr{H}^{S}$ is generated by objects which are compact in $\mathscr{H}$ . The assertion that $\mathscr{H}^{S,\perp}=\mathscr{H}_{S}$ follows from the fact that you can check whether $L_{w}$ appears as a composition factor of $x\in\mathscr{H}^{\heartsuit}$ after applying $\pi^{!}$ . This also shows that $\pi^{!}(\mathscr{H}_{S})\subseteq(\mathscr{O}_{0})_{S}$ .

It remains to show that $\pi^{!}(\mathscr{H}^{S})\subseteq(\mathscr{O}_{0})^{S}$ . We need to show that $\pi^{!}\pi_{!}P_{w}\in(\mathscr{O}_{0})^{S}$ for $w\notin S$ . It suffices to show that

$$ \Hom(\pi^{!}\pi_{!}P_{w},\mathscr{F})=0 $$

for all $\mathscr{F}\in(\mathscr{O}_{0})_{S}$ . Because $\pi^{!}\pi_{!}P_{w}$ is compact, we can assume that $\mathscr{F}=L_{v}$ for $v\in S$ . By adjunction

$$ \Hom(\pi^{!}\pi_{!}P_{w},L_{v})=\Hom(\pi^{*}\pi_{!}P_{w},L_{v})[-2\dim T]=\Hom(P_{w},\pi^{!}\pi_{*}L_{v})[-2\dim T]. $$

Since

$$ \pi^{!}\pi_{*}L_{v}\simeq C_{*}^{BM}(T)\otimes L_{v} $$

the result follows. ∎

#### 4.1.4.

Recall the notion of two-sided cells (already introduced in §1.2.3): if $\mathscr{H}_{w}^{\mathrm{access}}$ refers to the smallest two-sided ideal of $\mathscr{H}$ containing $L_{w}$ and stable under colimits and shifts, then we say that $v\leq_{LR}w$ if $L_{v}\in\mathscr{H}_{w}^{\mathrm{access}}$ . This defines a preorder on $W$ and the two-sided cells of $W$ are the corresponding partition: $w$ and $v$ lie in the same two-sided cell if $w\leq_{LR}v$ and $v\leq_{LR}w$ .

Let $c$ denote a two sided-cell in $W$ . Let $W_{\leq c}$ , $W_{<c}$ denote the subsets of $w\in W$ such that $w\leq_{LR}c$ and $w<_{LR}c$ , respectively. Denote the corresponding localizations of $\mathscr{H}$ by

$$ \mathscr{H}_{\leq c}\text{ and }\mathscr{H}_{<c}, $$

respectively.

#### Proposition 4.1.4.

$\mathscr{H}_{\leq c}$ and $\mathscr{H}_{<c}$ are monoidal two-sided ideals in $\mathscr{H}$ .

#### Proof.

If $S$ is a subset of $W$ , then because $\mathscr{H}_{S}$ is stable under colimits and $\mathscr{H}$ is generated by $L_{w}$ for $w\in W$ , one can show that $\mathscr{H}_{S}$ is a two-sided ideal in $\mathscr{H}$ just by showing that $L_{w}*(-)$ and $(-)*L_{w}$ preserve $\mathscr{H}_{S}$ . Every object $x\in\mathscr{H}_{S}$ can be written as the limit of its truncations for the t-structure

$$ x=\lim_{n}\tau_{\leq n}x, $$

and each $\tau_{\leq n}x$ can be written as a colimit of $L_{v}$ with $v\in S$ . Because $L_{w}$ is left- and right-dualizable and $\mathscr{H}_{S}$ is stable under limits as well as colimits, it suffices to show that $L_{w}*L_{v}$ and $L_{v}*L_{w}$ lie in $\mathscr{H}_{S}$ for all $v\in S$ . This is a direct consequence of the definition of two-sided cells (see §4.1.4). ∎

#### 4.1.5.

It follows from Proposition 4.1.3, Proposition 4.1.4, Proposition 2.1.0, and Proposition 2.1.0 that we obtain a system of semiorthogonal decompositions

$$ \mathscr{H}_{\not\leq c}\rightleftarrows\mathscr{H}\rightleftarrows\mathscr{H}_{\leq c} $$

where the subcategories of $\mathscr{H}$ admit monoidal structures making them semi-rigid monoidal categories, and the localization and colocalization functors are monoidal.

If we let $\mathscr{H}_{c}$ denote the left-orthogonal to $\mathscr{H}_{<c}$ inside of $\mathscr{H}_{\leq c}$ , then it follows from Proposition 2.1.0 and Proposition 2.1.0 that $\mathscr{H}_{c}$ admits a unique monoidal structure such that the projection $\mathscr{H}\to\mathscr{H}_{c}$ is monoidal, and with respect to this monoidal structure $\mathscr{H}_{c}$ has the structure of a semi-rigid category. We also note that

$$ \mathscr{H}_{c}\simeq\mathscr{H}_{\leq c}\underset{\mathscr{H}}{\otimes}\mathscr{H}_{\not<c} $$

so we may think of the categories $\mathscr{H}_{c}$ as the associated-graded pieces of the system of semiorthogonal decompositions (18).

Let’s return to the case of $SL_{2}$ . Let $c$ denote the cell $\left\{1\right\}\subseteq W$ . Then $\mathscr{H}_{c}$ is the subcategory of $\mathscr{H}$ generated by $\pi_{!}P_{1}$ .

$$ \pi_{i}\End(\pi_{!}P_{1})=\begin{cases}k&i=0,1\\
0&\text{otherwise}\end{cases} $$

so it follows that $\mathscr{H}_{c}$ identifies with $\QCoh(\Omega\mathbf{A}^{1})$ as a plain dg category. ### 4.2. An action of the monoid $\mathbf{A}^{1}$

#### 4.2.1.

In [GLR26], we introduced a sheaf theory $\Sh(-)^{\mathrm{relev}}$ which is defined on schemes over $\mathbf{F}_{q}$ . If $X_{0}$ is a scheme over $\mathbf{F}_{q}$ whose base-change to $\overline{\mathbf{F}}_{q}$ is $X$ , then in keeping with the convention of loc. cit. we somewhat abusively denote the value of $\Sh(-)^{\mathrm{relev}}$ on $X_{0}$ by $\Sh(X)^{\mathrm{relev}}$ . The definition of $\Sh(X)^{\mathrm{relev}}$ is as follows: the given $\mathbf{F}_{q}$ structure on $X$ equips this scheme with a geometric Frobenius endomorphism $\mathrm{Frob}$ , and

$$ \Sh(X)^{\mathrm{relev}}\subseteq\Sh(X) $$

is the subcategory generated under colimits and shifts by irreducible perverse sheaves $\mathscr{F}\in\mathrm{Perv}(X)$ such that for some $n\geq 1$ there exists an isomorphism $\mathscr{F}\simeq(\mathrm{Frob}^{n})^{*}\mathscr{F}$ .

The important feature of $\Sh(X)^{\mathrm{relev}}$ is that it admits an action of a pro-algebraic group which we will denote $\mathbf{W}$ .55 5 This is the group which is denoted $\mathbf{Z}^{\mathrm{alg,wt}}$ in loc. cit. This action is constructed using the theory of weights for $\ell$ -adic sheaves on varieties over finite fields and it has the property that $(\Sh(X)^{\mathrm{relev}})^{\mathbf{W}}$ is the category $\Sh(X)^{\mathrm{Weil},\mathrm{wt}}$ (introduced in loc. cit.) which is a minor variant of the category of mixed sheaves (sometimes we will call an object of $\Sh(X)^{\mathrm{Weil},\mathrm{wt}}$ a strongly mixed sheaf). If $\mathrm{Weil}_{q}\subseteq\overline{\mathbf{Q}}^{\times}$ denotes the subgroup of $q$ -Weil numbers, then $\mathbf{W}$ is the Cartier dual of ${\mathbf{G}_{m}}^{\wedge}_{\mathrm{Weil}_{q}}$ . The homomorphism

$$ \mathrm{wt}:{\mathbf{G}_{m}}^{\wedge}_{\mathrm{Weil}_{q}}\to\mathbf{Z} $$

which sends a connected component of ${\mathbf{G}_{m}}^{\wedge}_{\mathrm{Weil}_{q}}$ to the weight of its underlying Weil number gives rise to a distinguished subgroup ${\mathbf{G}_{m}}\subseteq\mathbf{W}$ after applying Cartier duality. The inclusion

$$ {\mathbf{G}_{m}}^{\wedge}_{\mathrm{Weil}_{q}}\subseteq{\mathbf{G}_{m}} $$

gives rise to a homomorphism $\mathrm{Frob}:\mathbf{Z}\to\mathbf{W}$ whose image is Zariski dense. One of the defining features of the action of $\mathbf{W}$ on $\Sh(X)^{\mathrm{relev}}$ is that the element $\mathrm{Frob}\in\mathbf{W}$ acts by pullback along geometric Frobenius.

#### 4.2.2.

Another feature of the action of $\mathbf{W}$ on $\Sh(X)^{\mathrm{relev}}$ is that the action of the weight ${\mathbf{G}_{m}}$ extends to an action of the commutative monoid scheme $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ . In terms of Proposition 3.0.1 the category $(\Sh(X)^{\mathrm{relev}})^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}$ is a minor variant of the category of graded mixed sheaves introduced in [HL25], and the subcategory $(\Sh(X)^{\mathrm{relev}})^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}_{\leq 0}$ is the category generated under colimits and shifts by perverse sheaves which are weight $\leq 0$ in the sense of [BBD82] (this category was considered previously in [Mor08]).

#### 4.2.3. Warning

The category $(\Sh(X)^{\mathrm{relev}})^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}_{\leq 0}$ is not the derived category of mixed sheaves of weight $\leq 0$ in the sense of [BBD82]. Unlike the category defined in loc. cit., the category $(\Sh(X)^{\mathrm{relev}})^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}_{\leq 0}$ is stable under shifts. This is advantageous for certain purposes, but it has the following drawback: if $f$ is a smooth proper map, then $f_{*}$ does not preserve weights in our sense.

#### 4.2.4.

Let $f:X\to Y$ be a smooth morphism between schemes. Define the perverse pullback functor

$$ f^{!*}:\Sh(Y)^{\mathrm{relev}}\to\Sh(X)^{\mathrm{relev}} $$

by

$$ f^{!*}=f^{*}[\dim(X/Y)]=f^{!}[-\dim(X/Y)]. $$

By construction, this functor is t-exact for the perverse t-structure. If we choose a square-root of $q$ , we can equip $f^{1/2}$ with the structure of equivariance for $\mathbf{W}$ as follows: consider the functor (which we will also denote $f^{1/2}$ ) from $\Sh(Y)^{\mathrm{Weil},\mathrm{wt}}$ to $\Sh(X)^{\mathrm{Weil},\mathrm{wt}}$ defined by

$$ f^{!*}=f^{*}(\tfrac{\dim(X/Y)}{2})[\dim(X/Y)]=f^{!}(-\tfrac{\dim(X/Y)}{2})[-\dim(X/Y)]. $$

Then the functor between the categories of relevant sheaves arises as the de-equivariantization of this functor between the categories of strongly mixed sheaves, equipping it with equivariance data for $\mathbf{W}$ . It is easy to see that the functor $f^{!*}$ is $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ -equivariant for the $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ -action of §4.2.2.

If $\mathscr{Y}$ is an Artin stack, then define

$$ \Sh(\mathscr{Y})^{\mathrm{relev}}=\lim_{Y\to\mathscr{Y}}\Sh(Y)^{\mathrm{relev}} $$

where the limit is taken over all schemes $Y$ mapping smoothly to $\mathscr{Y}$ and the transition maps are the perverse pullback functors. In other words, $\Sh(\mathscr{Y})^{\mathrm{relev}}$ is the full subcategory of $\Sh(\mathscr{Y})$ consisting of sheaves whose pullback to some (equiv. any) smooth cover is relevant. Taking the limit (19) internally to categories acted on by $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ defines a natural $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ -action on $\Sh(\mathscr{Y})^{\mathrm{relev}}$ . This $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ -action has the property that if $f:Y\to\mathscr{Y}$ is a smooth cover, then an object $\mathscr{F}$ of $\mathscr{Y}$ is in $\mathrm{Shv}(\mathscr{Y})^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}_{\leq 0}$ if and only if its pullback to $Y$ is, and similarly for $\mathrm{Shv}(\mathscr{Y})^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}_{\geq 0}$ .

#### Proposition 4.2.4.

If $\mathscr{Y}=N\backslash G/B$ or $\mathscr{Y}=B\backslash G/B$ , then

$$ \Sh(\mathscr{Y})^{\mathrm{relev}}=\Sh(\mathscr{Y}). $$

#### Proof.

These categories are generated by the IC sheaves $L_{w}$ , whose pullbacks to $G/B$ are relevant. ∎

#### 4.2.5.

The above discussion shows that $\mathscr{H}$ acquires an action of the monoid $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ . Since the action of ${\mathbf{G}_{m}}\subseteq\mathbf{A}^{1}$ is compatible with six functors, the monoidal structure on $\mathscr{H}$ is compatible with this ${\mathbf{G}_{m}}$ action. However, we caution that because of the behavior described in §4.2.3, the $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ -action on $\mathscr{H}$ is not compatible with its monoidal structure.

#### Proposition 4.2.5.

For any $S\subseteq W$ , the category $\mathscr{H}_{S}$ is stable under the $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ on $\mathscr{H}$ .

#### Proof.

The is follows by the arguments of [GLR26, §3.1]. In a little more detail, to show that $\mathscr{H}_{S}$ is stable under the action of ${\mathbf{G}_{m}}$ , then as in the proof of [GLR26, Lemma 3.1.4] it suffices to show that the comonad

$$ \mathscr{H}\xrightarrow{\mathrm{Av}_{\mathbf{G}_{m}}}\mathscr{H}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}\xrightarrow{\mathrm{oblv}}\mathscr{H} $$

preserves $\mathscr{H}_{S}$ . The comonad is t-exact (this can be checked after applying $\mathrm{oblv}$ to $\mathscr{O}_{0}$ , where it follows from the corresponding statement for schemes, which is the content of [GLR26, §2.6]), so it’s enough to check on objects in the heart. Since the comonad commutes with colimits, it suffices to show that it sends $L_{w}$ to an object of $\mathscr{H}_{S}$ for all $w\in S$ . Now each $L_{w}$ admits the structure of a strongly mixed sheaf, so the value of the comonad on $L_{w}$ is simply $\mathscr{O}_{\mathbf{G}_{m}}\otimes L_{w}\in\mathscr{H}_{S}$ .

Once we know that $\mathscr{H}_{S}$ is stable under the action of ${\mathbf{G}_{m}}$ , as in [GLR26, Proposition 3.1.7] to prove that it is stable under $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ it suffices to show that $\mathscr{H}_{S}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}$ is preserved by the weight truncation functors on $\mathscr{H}^{\mathbf{G}_{m}}$ . The weight truncation functors are t-exact (again this follows by applying $\mathrm{oblv}$ to $\mathscr{O}_{0}$ ), so it suffices to check this for objects of the heart. Now the result follows because

$$ \tau_{\leq i}L_{w}=\begin{cases}L_{w}&i\geq 0\\
0&i<0\end{cases} $$

∎

By Proposition 4.2.5 the inclusions

$$ \mathscr{H}_{<c}\to\mathscr{H}_{\leq c}\to\mathscr{H} $$

are $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ -equivariant. The left adjoints of these inclusions are left-lax $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ -equivariant, but we caution that the left adjoints are not strictly $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ -equivariant. By the compatibility of the $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ action on $\mathscr{H}$ with smooth pullbacks (see §4.2.4) and Proposition 4.1.3 we see that the forgetful functor $\mathscr{H}_{\leq c}\to(\mathscr{O}_{0})_{\leq c}$ is $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ -equivariant. By writing

$$ \mathscr{H}_{c}\simeq\mathscr{H}_{\leq c}/\mathscr{H}_{<c} $$

$\mathscr{H}_{c}$ acquires an action of $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ such that the projection $\mathscr{H}_{\leq c}\to\mathscr{H}_{c}$ is tautologically $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ -equivariant. We caution that the inclusion $\mathscr{H}_{c}\to\mathscr{H}_{\leq c}$ is only left-lax $\mathbf{A}^{1}$ -equivariant.

#### 4.2.6. Example

If we set $G=SL_{2}$ and take $c=\left\{1\right\}$ , then like in §4.1.2, one can calculate that

$$ H_{i}(\tau_{<c}(L_{1}))\simeq\begin{cases}L_{s}\left\langle-2i+1\right\rangle&i\geq 1\\
0&i<1\end{cases} $$

and

$$ H_{i}(\tau_{c}(L_{1}))\simeq\begin{cases}L_{s}\left\langle-2i-1\right\rangle&i>0\\
\nabla_{s}\left\langle-1\right\rangle&i=0\\
0&i<0\end{cases} $$
